title: Evaporation and condensation with particles: what speeds up drying, and how the water cycle works

summary.text: A tumbler of water at room temperature has no flame under it, yet its level drops a little every day. The particles of the water move at many different speeds. The fastest ones at the surface escape into the air as water vapour. That is evaporation. Warmth, a wider surface, moving air and dry air all speed it up. When particles of vapour slow down on something cool, they join again as drops. That is condensation. Your child measures how the size of the surface changes evaporation. They find out why evaporation cools the water left behind, and they explain the water cycle with particles.
summary.art: A steel plate, a bowl and a tumbler of water in a row under a ceiling fan, with a zoom circle on the plate showing a few fast particles leaving the water surface.

intro.hook: After a head bath, hair left loose dries in about an hour. The same hair tied in a tight plait can still be damp at bedtime. The hair, the water and the air are the same. So why does the plait stay wet?
intro.text: Water can leave only from a surface that touches the air. Loose hair has a very large surface, and a plait hides most of that surface inside. In this unit you find out what happens at the surface of water. You measure how much more water leaves a wide plate than a narrow tumbler. You find out why hot milk cools faster in a davara than in a tumbler. Then you follow particles of water from the sea up to a cloud and back down as rain.
intro.art: Two girls on a sunny balcony after a head bath, one with loose hair spread over a towel on her shoulders and one with a tight wet plait.

outcomes: By the end I can explain evaporation with particles: the fastest particles at the surface escape as water vapour.
By the end I can explain condensation with particles, and say why it is the reverse of evaporation.
By the end I can name four things that speed up evaporation, and explain each one with particles.
By the end I can show with my own measurements that a bigger surface loses more water.
By the end I can explain why evaporation cools the water left behind, using evidence from The Oil Lid.
By the end I can tell evaporation from boiling, and say what the bubbles in boiling water are.
By the end I can explain the water cycle with particles, and name the kinds of precipitation.
By the end I can plan a fair test that changes only one thing, and say what my results show.

terms.meaning: One of the tiny pieces that every substance is made of. Particles are far too small to see, even with a school microscope. A particle of water is also called a water molecule.
terms.example: One teaspoon of water holds more particles than there are grains of sand on all the beaches of the Earth.
terms.art: A drop of water with a zoom circle showing many tiny round particles packed together.

terms.meaning: A way of explaining what substances do by picturing their particles. In a solid the particles are held in place. In a liquid they touch and slide past each other. In a gas they are far apart and fly freely.
terms.example: The particle model explains why a puddle dries: particles leave the liquid one by one and fly off as a gas.
terms.art: Three boxes of dots: neat rows for a solid, a jumbled crowd for a liquid, and a few far-apart dots with arrows for a gas.

terms.meaning: A liquid turning into a gas at its surface. It happens at any temperature, because some particles at the surface are always moving fast enough to escape.
terms.example: A wet floor dries after mopping. The water has evaporated into the air of the room.
terms.art: A freshly mopped floor with a few arrows rising from a wet patch that is shrinking.

terms.meaning: Water as a gas. Its particles are far apart and mixed in with the particles of the air, so it cannot be seen.
terms.example: The air in your room holds water vapour now. You see it only when it turns back into drops on a cold bottle.
terms.art: A room that looks empty, with a zoom circle showing a few water particles among many air particles.

terms.meaning: A gas turning into a liquid. Particles of water vapour slow down on something cool and stick together as drops.
terms.example: The inside of a pot lid is covered in drops when rice is cooking. The vapour condensed on the cooler lid.
terms.art: A hand lifting the lid of a rice pot, with drops running down the inside of the lid.

terms.meaning: A change from solid to liquid, liquid to gas, or back again. The particles stay the same. Only how they move and how close they are changes.
terms.example: Melting, freezing, evaporation and condensation are the four changes of state of water at home.
terms.art: A triangle of three pictures, an ice cube, a tumbler of water and a faint wisp of vapour, joined by arrows.

terms.meaning: A change that can be undone, so that you get the same substance back.
terms.example: Water evaporates from the sea, condenses in a cloud and falls as rain. It is the same water all the way.
terms.art: Two arrows in a loop between a puddle and a cloud.

terms.meaning: The size of the surface of a thing. For water in a vessel, it is the size of the top of the water. That is where the water touches the air. It is measured in square centimetres.
terms.example: Water in a wide plate has a much bigger surface area than the same water in a tumbler.
terms.art: A plate and a tumbler seen from above, with the round water surface of each shaded.

terms.meaning: A number that tells how fast the particles of a thing are moving on average. The faster they move, the higher the temperature. It is measured in degrees Celsius.
terms.example: The particles in hot rasam move faster on average than the particles in cold buttermilk.
terms.art: A thermometer standing in a tumbler, with a zoom circle of particles drawn with short and long speed arrows.

terms.meaning: One number that stands for a whole group of numbers. To find it, add all the numbers and divide by how many there are.
terms.example: Four particles have speeds 2, 3, 3 and 6. The total is 14, so the average speed is 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5.
terms.art: Four dots with the numbers 2, 3, 3 and 6 above them, and one line drawn at 3.5.

terms.meaning: How much water evaporates in a given time, such as millilitres in a day.
terms.example: On a hot, windy day the rate of evaporation from a wet towel is high. The towel dries in under an hour.
terms.art: Two measuring glasses a day apart, the second with a lower water level and an arrow marking the drop.

terms.meaning: How much water vapour is in the air. Humid air already holds a lot of vapour, and dry air holds little.
terms.example: Mumbai in July is very humid, so clothes on the line stay damp. Jaipur in May is dry, so they dry fast.
terms.art: Two washing lines, one under grey monsoon clouds with dripping clothes and one under a clear hot sky.

terms.meaning: Air that holds as much water vapour as it can at that temperature. In saturated air, as many particles land back on a wet thing as leave it, so nothing dries.
terms.example: The air inside a closed, half-full water bottle is saturated. The water level in the bottle does not fall.
terms.art: A capped plastic bottle half full of water, with tiny drops on the inside wall above the water.

terms.meaning: The temperature at which the vapour in the air starts to condense. The more vapour the air holds, the higher its dew point.
terms.example: On a humid day in Kochi the dew point may be 25 degrees. A glass of cool water at 20 degrees mists over at once.
terms.art: A steel tumbler of iced water with a thermometer in it and a band of mist on the outside.

terms.meaning: Fast evaporation that happens all through a liquid, with bubbles of gas forming inside it. Water boils only when it is hot enough.
terms.example: Water for tea boils in the pan. The big bubbles that rise from the bottom are full of water vapour.
terms.art: A steel pan of boiling water on a stove with large bubbles rising from the bottom.

terms.meaning: The temperature at which a liquid boils. For pure water at sea level, it is 100 degrees Celsius.
terms.example: Water in an open pan in Chennai stays at 100 degrees however long it boils.
terms.art: A thermometer in a pan of bubbling water, reading 100.

terms.meaning: The cooling of a liquid, or of whatever it is on, as the liquid evaporates. The fastest particles leave, so the ones left behind are slower on average.
terms.example: Sweat evaporating from your skin cools you after a game of kabaddi.
terms.art: A child wiping a sweaty forehead after a game, with small arrows leaving the skin.

terms.meaning: The round journey of water. Water evaporates from the sea and the land and condenses into clouds. It falls as rain or snow and flows back to the sea.
terms.example: Rain that falls on the Western Ghats may have evaporated from the Arabian Sea a few days before.
terms.art: A sea, a cloud, rain on hills and a river, joined in a loop by four arrows.

terms.meaning: Any water that falls from clouds to the ground: rain, drizzle, snow or hail.
terms.example: Shimla gets snow in January, and Hyderabad sometimes gets hail in April. Both are precipitation.
terms.art: Three small panels: rain on a street, snow on a hill roof, and hailstones on a road.

terms.meaning: Anything in a test that could be changed. In a fair test you change one variable and keep all the others the same.
terms.example: In the Wide or Narrow test, the variable you change is the size of the water surface. The amount of water stays the same.
terms.art: Two cloths on a line with a label 'change this' on one thing and 'keep the same' on three others.

explanations.concept: Evaporation with particles: the fastest ones at the surface escape
explanations.definition: Evaporation is a liquid turning into a gas at its surface. The particles of a liquid move at many different speeds. A particle at the surface that is moving fast enough breaks away from its neighbours. It flies off into the air.
explanations.description: The particles of liquid water touch each other and hold on to each other. They also move all the time, bumping and sliding. After each bump a particle may be moving faster or slower than before. So at any moment a few particles are very fast, most are in the middle, and a few are slow. Deep inside the water a fast particle only bumps into more water. At the surface a fast particle can break free. It becomes a particle of water vapour, a gas, and mixes with the air. This goes on at every temperature, with no flame and no sunshine. That is why a tumbler of water left on a shelf slowly goes down.
examples: In the Shake the Plate activity in this unit, whole chana, which are chickpeas, in a steel plate stand for particles of water. Only the chana that reached the rim with enough speed jumped out. Most of the chana stayed in the plate.
A wet steel plate left on the drying rack is dry by evening, though nobody heated it.
Ink left in an open bottle dries up over the summer holidays.
explanations.art: A zoom view of a water surface: a crowd of particles with short and long arrows, and two long-arrowed particles at the top flying off into the air.

explanations.concept: Water leaves only at the surface, so a bigger surface loses more
explanations.definition: Evaporation happens where water meets air. The more surface the water has, the more particles are at the surface at any moment. So more of them leave each second.
explanations.description: Pour the same water into a wide plate and a narrow tumbler. The plate has many more particles at its surface, so many more leave each minute. Double the surface, and about double the water leaves in the same time. The amount of water underneath makes no difference to how fast it leaves. A deep lake and a shallow puddle in the same weather lose about the same depth of water each day. The puddle is gone first only because it had little depth to lose. A tall vessel loses a little less than its surface suggests. Damp air collects above the water inside its walls, and some particles land back.
examples: In the Wide or Narrow experiment in this unit, the plate's surface was about four times the bowl's. The plate lost about four times as much water.
Wet hair left loose dries much sooner than the same hair in a plait.
Farmers in Guntur spread red chillies in a thin layer on the ground, and never dry them in a heap.
Salt makers in Thoothukudi let sea water into wide, shallow pans, not deep tanks.
explanations.art: The same amount of water drawn in a wide shallow plate and in a tall narrow tumbler, with many arrows leaving the plate and only a few leaving the tumbler.

explanations.definition: Warming water makes its particles move faster on average. So more of the particles at the surface are fast enough to escape each second.
explanations.description: Heat is energy, and it goes into the movement of the particles. In cool water only a few particles at the surface are fast enough to leave. In warm water many more are. So warm water evaporates much faster than cool water, long before it boils. The Sun warms the top of the sea, a wet road and a wet shirt in this way. Warmth helps in a second way too. Warm air can carry more water vapour before it is saturated. So fewer particles land back on the wet thing.
examples: Clothes on a terrace in Madurai dry in an hour at noon in May. In December they take half a day.
In the Fast Ones Leave game in this unit, adding 1 to every speed for the Sun round let more particles reach the escape speed.
A puddle on a tar road vanishes sooner than a puddle of the same size under a tree.
explanations.art: Two tumblers side by side, one in sunshine and one in shade, with a zoom circle on each showing longer speed arrows in the sunny one.

explanations.concept: Why moving air and dry air speed up evaporation
explanations.definition: Particles that have escaped can land back on the water. Moving air carries them away, and dry air has few of them to begin with. In both cases fewer particles land back, so the water goes down faster.
explanations.description: Evaporation is a two-way traffic. Particles leave the surface, and particles of vapour from the air land back on it. What we see is the difference between the two. In still air the escaped particles collect just above the surface, and many land back. A fan or a breeze sweeps them away and brings air with less vapour. In humid air, such as Kolkata's in the monsoon, the air already holds a lot of vapour. Nearly as many particles land as leave. Inside a closed bottle the two become equal. The water level stays the same, although particles still leave and land every moment.
examples: In the Tilting Hanger experiment in this unit, the cloth under the fan lost more water than the same cloth in still air.
In the Wide or Narrow experiment in this unit, the closed jar lost no water at all in a whole day.
A towel hung in a closed bathroom after a bath stays wet. The same towel on the balcony dries.
explanations.art: A wet cloth under a ceiling fan, with arrows carrying escaped particles sideways, beside a wet cloth in a closed bathroom with particles going both ways.

explanations.concept: Why evaporation cools what is left: temperature is an average
explanations.definition: The temperature of water tells how fast its particles move on average. Evaporation takes away the fastest particles. The ones left behind are slower on average, so the water is cooler.
explanations.description: A thermometer gives one number for a whole tumbler of water. But the particles in the tumbler have many different speeds. The number stands for their average. When the fastest particles escape, the average of the rest goes down. A class's average height goes down in the same way if the tallest children leave the room. The water then takes in heat from whatever it touches: your skin, a clay pot, the air. That is why evaporation cools things. Evaporating one teaspoon of sweat takes away enough heat to cool a litre of water by nearly 3 degrees.
examples: In the Oil Lid experiment in this unit, the open bowl of hot water cooled faster than the bowl sealed with oil.
In the Fast Ones Leave game in this unit, the average speed in the pot fell whenever the 5s and 6s at the surface escaped.
Hot coffee poured back and forth between a davara and a tumbler cools in a minute.
A dog pants on a hot day. Water evaporates from her tongue and cools her blood.
explanations.art: A row of twelve particles with speed numbers above them, the two highest circled and leaving, and the average line of the rest drawn lower.

explanations.concept: Condensation with particles: the reverse of evaporation
explanations.definition: Condensation is a gas turning into a liquid. Particles of water vapour that touch something cool lose energy and slow down. They stick to each other and to the surface. Many of them together make a drop.
explanations.description: Particles of water vapour fly about at around 600 metres a second, faster than a passenger jet. When one hits a cold tumbler, it gives some of its energy to the steel and slows down. A slow particle cannot break away again, so it stays. More particles join it, and soon there is a drop big enough to see. Condensation is evaporation in reverse. Evaporation takes heat in, and condensation gives the same amount of heat back out. That is why steam burns the skin more badly than boiling water. In 1958 the weather scientists Joanne Simpson (then Malkus) and Herbert Riehl argued that this heat powers the tall towers of rain cloud in the tropics.
examples: Mist forms on a steel tumbler of cold buttermilk, but only as high as the buttermilk inside.
Your warm breath makes a misty patch on a cold window, and the patch evaporates again in seconds.
The outside of a cold water bottle taken from the fridge is wet within a minute in Chennai in August.
explanations.art: A zoom view of a cold steel surface: fast vapour particles arriving with long arrows and slow ones stuck together in a small drop.

explanations.concept: Four changes of state, and what each needs
explanations.definition: Water changes state in four everyday ways. Melting and evaporation need heat to go in. Freezing and condensation happen when heat goes out. All four can be undone.
explanations.description: Ice melts when heat goes in and its particles shake loose from their places. Water freezes when heat goes out and the particles lock into place again. Water evaporates when particles at the surface take in enough energy to fly off. Vapour condenses when its particles lose that energy. In every change the particles themselves stay the same, so no water is made and none is destroyed. Seal a little water in a bottle. The bottle has the same mass before and after the water evaporates and condenses inside it.
examples: Melting: an ice cube in a tumbler of nimbu pani.
Freezing: water in an ice tray in the freezer.
Evaporation: a wet swimming costume drying on a line.
Condensation: drops under the lid of a tiffin box packed with hot idlis.
explanations.art: A triangle with ice, water and vapour at its corners and four arrows labelled melting, freezing, evaporation and condensation, red for heat going in and blue for heat going out.

explanations.concept: Boiling is not the same as evaporation
explanations.definition: Evaporation happens only at the surface, at any temperature. Boiling happens all through the liquid, only at the boiling point, with bubbles of vapour forming inside the liquid.
explanations.description: Heat a pan of water and watch. Tiny bubbles appear on the bottom and walls while the water is only warm. These are air that was dissolved in the water. Much later, at 100 degrees Celsius, big bubbles form at the hot bottom and rise. These are water vapour: water that has turned into a gas inside the liquid. Once water is boiling, more heat does not make it hotter. The heat goes into turning more water into vapour. The white cloud above the pan is the vapour condensing into tiny drops as it meets cooler air. Real water vapour is invisible.
examples: In the What Is in the Bubbles? activity in this unit, the first small bubbles came out long before the water boiled.
Rasam left simmering with no lid slowly gets less. The missing rasam left as vapour.
A wet floor dries at 30 degrees without ever boiling.
explanations.art: Two pans side by side: one of warm water with a few arrows leaving the surface, and one boiling with large bubbles rising from the bottom.

explanations.concept: The water cycle explained with particles
explanations.definition: The water cycle is evaporation and condensation on the scale of the whole Earth. Sunlight gives particles at the surface of the sea enough energy to leave. High up, where the air is cold, they slow down and join into the drops of a cloud.
explanations.description: Sunlight warms the top of the sea. The fastest water particles escape, and the salt stays behind. The vapour mixes into the air, and warm, damp air rises. As the air rises it cools, by about 5 to 10 degrees for every kilometre. When it is cooled to its dew point, the vapour particles slow down. They stick to specks of dust, salt or smoke. Each speck grows into a cloud drop about a fiftieth of a millimetre wide. About a million cloud drops must join to make one raindrop. Drops that are heavy enough fall as rain. In very cold clouds the water falls as snow or hail. Rain runs into rivers and soaks into the ground, and most of it reaches the sea again.
examples: The south-west monsoon carries vapour from the Arabian Sea. It condenses as the air is pushed up the Western Ghats.
The sea loses more than a metre of depth to evaporation every year, about 3 millimetres a day. Rain and rivers put it back.
A particle of water stays in the air for about 9 days, on average, before it falls.
A tree is part of the cycle. A large oak tree can send about 150,000 litres of water into the air from its leaves in a year.
explanations.art: A cut-away picture of sea, sky and hills with six zoom circles: particles leaving the sea, mixing in air, cooling, joining on a dust speck, falling as a raindrop, and flowing in a river.

explanations.concept: Dew point: how to tell how much vapour is in the air
explanations.definition: The dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled before its vapour starts to condense. Humid air has a high dew point, and dry air has a low one.
explanations.description: Vapour particles in warm air are too fast to stick. Cool the air, or bring it against a cold surface, and at some temperature they begin to stick. That temperature is the dew point. You can find it with a steel tumbler, a thermometer and ice. Cool the water slowly and read the thermometer when the first mist appears. Weather offices report the dew point every day. Clouds form at the height where rising air has cooled to its dew point. That is why the bottoms of many clouds are flat.
examples: In the Find the Dew Point activity in this unit, the mist appeared at a higher temperature in a steamy bathroom than in the bedroom.
Dew forms on parked scooters in Bengaluru on clear winter nights, when the metal cools below the dew point.
On a humid summer day in Chennai the dew point can be about 25 degrees. On a cold, dry winter morning in Delhi it can be 5 degrees or lower.
explanations.art: A steel tumbler with a thermometer and floating ice, a clear band at the top of the outside and a misty band below.

explanations.definition: Many living beings cool themselves by letting water evaporate from their bodies. The water takes heat away with it.
explanations.description: Humans cool mainly by sweating. A person working hard in the heat can lose more than a litre of sweat in an hour. The sweat cools the body only if it evaporates. On a very humid day it drips off, and the body stays hot. A dog has few sweat glands, so she pants and lets water evaporate from her tongue and mouth. Honeybees carry water into the hive on hot days. They spread it in thin films and fan it with their wings, and the hive cools. Plants lose water vapour through tiny holes in their leaves, and this cools the leaf. The plant opens and closes these holes, and so controls how much water leaves.
examples: After running, you cool faster under a fan, because the moving air carries away the vapour from your sweat.
A crow on a hot terrace in Nagpur holds her beak open and pants.
A leaf in full sunshine stays cooler than a stone beside it.
explanations.art: Four small panels: a sweating child drinking water, a panting dog, bees fanning at a hive entrance, and a leaf with a zoom on a tiny open hole.

explanations.concept: Should lakes and canals be covered to stop evaporation?
explanations.description: India's reservoirs and canals lose a great deal of water to evaporation each summer. Covering the surface cuts the loss. In 2012 Gujarat roofed a stretch of a Narmada canal with solar panels. In 2015 the city of Los Angeles floated 96 million black plastic balls on one reservoir. Floating solar panels now sit on reservoirs in Telangana and Kerala. But a cover changes the water under it. People who study this do not agree on how far to go.
examples: Canal-top solar panels in Gujarat shade the water and make electricity at the same time.
A study in 2018 found that making the Los Angeles balls used a lot of water too. The balls must float for years to save more than they cost.
Farmers cover the soil round young plants with dry leaves or straw. This is called mulch, and it slows evaporation from the soil.

perspectives.explanation: Every litre that evaporates from a reservoir is a litre lost to a town or a field. Covers and shade save water where it is most scarce, so we should use them widely.
A cover blocks light and slows the mixing of air into the water. Water plants, fish and birds lose their home. Cover canals and tanks, but leave living lakes open.
Evaporation cools the land and feeds the rain. Covering a few reservoirs changes little. But the saved water is small beside what better pipes and less waste would save.

explanations.art: A long canal roofed with solar panels crossing dry fields, with a kingfisher perched on the edge of the last panel.

explanations.concept: Can light knock water particles out without heating the water?
explanations.description: For two hundred years, evaporation has been explained by heat alone: warm particles move faster, and the fastest leave. In 2023 a group led by Gang Chen at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology reported something odd. Under certain light, their wet materials lost water faster than the heat in the light could explain. Green light worked best. They suggested that light can knock small clusters of water particles straight out of the surface. They named this the photomolecular effect. Other laboratories are still testing whether it is real. If it is, it may happen in clouds and fog as well.
examples: Some measurements suggest that clouds take in a little more sunlight than theory predicts. This effect might explain why.
If the effect is real, it could make machines that dry things or clean salty water using less energy.
explanations.art: A laboratory bench with a dish of wet gel under a green lamp, and a scientist reading a balance beside it.

agreed.text: Evaporation happens only at the surface of a liquid, and at any temperature.
agreed.evidence: The same water goes down faster in a wide dish than in a narrow one. Wet things dry in a cool room, far below the boiling point.

agreed.text: The particles of a liquid at one temperature move at many different speeds.
agreed.evidence: James Clerk Maxwell worked this out for gases in 1860. In the 1920s, experiments with beams of atoms tested the spread of speeds he had predicted.

agreed.text: Evaporation cools the liquid that is left, and condensation gives the same heat out again.
agreed.evidence: Water wrapped in a wet cloth falls below the temperature of the room. Steam that condenses on skin gives out enough heat to burn.

agreed.text: Warmth, a bigger surface, moving air and dry air each make evaporation faster.
agreed.evidence: Each can be tested alone, with everything else kept the same. Weather stations across India measure daily evaporation from open pans.

agreed.text: Water vapour is a gas that mixes with the air. The air does not dissolve the water.
agreed.evidence: John Dalton found this in 1801. Water gives off the same amount of vapour into an empty space as into air.

agreed.text: The water cycle neither makes nor destroys water.
agreed.evidence: More than a metre of depth leaves the sea each year. The rain and river water that return to it match that loss.

challenging.claim: The bubbles in boiling water are air.
challenging.who: A very common belief among children and adults
challenging.for: Bubbles in a fish tank and in soda are gas that came from outside the water. Small bubbles do appear in a pan while the water is only warm, and those really are air.
challenging.against: The big bubbles at the boil keep coming for as long as the pan is heated. By then the dissolved air has long gone. If they were air, the water would not get less. They are water vapour, and the water level falls as they leave.
challenging.context: This card is about what is inside the bubbles of boiling water.

challenging.claim: More water evaporates from a full bucket than from a wet floor, because the bucket holds more water.
challenging.for: A bucket holds far more water than a thin wet film. It seems that a bigger amount should give off more.
challenging.against: Water leaves only from its surface. A mopped floor has a surface hundreds of times bigger than a bucket's. So it loses water hundreds of times faster. The floor is dry in minutes, and the bucket stays full for days.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the amount of water or the size of its surface decides how fast water evaporates.

challenging.claim: At one temperature, every particle of water moves at the same speed.
challenging.who: What a single thermometer reading seems to say
challenging.for: A thermometer gives one number for the whole tumbler. Stir the water and the number is the same everywhere.
challenging.against: If all the particles had the same speed, either all of them could escape or none could. Water would vanish in an instant or never dry. Slow, steady evaporation shows that only a few particles are fast enough at any moment.
challenging.context: This card is about what one temperature tells us about the particles of water.

challenging.claim: A cloud is a bag of water vapour that bursts when it is full.
challenging.who: A picture many children have, and the phrase 'cloudburst'
challenging.for: Clouds look like solid shapes with edges. Heavy rain can start very suddenly, as if something had split.
challenging.against: A cloud has no skin. It is air full of tiny liquid drops, too small to fall fast. Rain starts when drops join until they are heavy enough to fall. A cloudburst is very heavy rain from a tall cloud, and nothing bursts.
challenging.context: This card is about what a cloud is and how rain starts.

challenging.claim: Light can free water particles from a surface directly, without heating the water.
challenging.who: Gang Chen and his group at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in a paper from 2023
challenging.for: Their wet samples lost water faster under light than the heat in the light could explain. The effect changed with the colour of the light, which plain heating would not do.
challenging.against: The results are new, and other laboratories have not yet repeated them fully. Some scientists suggest other explanations, such as water in a gel evaporating more easily than plain water.
challenging.context: This card is about a new and unproven idea: that light, and not only heat, can cause evaporation.

big_questions.q: No single particle of water has a temperature of its own. So what does the temperature of a tumbler of water describe?
big_questions.hint: Think about the average height of a class. Does any one child have to be exactly that tall?

big_questions.q: Nobody chooses which particles leave. Yet an open bowl of hot water cools every time. How can chance give the same result each time?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Fast Ones Leave game in this unit. What happens to the average when only high numbers are removed?

big_questions.q: Evaporation and condensation are the same change, run in opposite directions. After a round trip, is the water the same water?
big_questions.hint: Think about what changes in a change of state, and what stays.

big_questions.q: The Sun lifts more than a metre of the sea into the sky each year, for free. A city pays for pumps to lift water to a tank. Who does the work in each case?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the energy comes from each time.

big_questions.q: A potter slows evaporation to save her pots. A farmer speeds it up to save her grain. Is fast drying good or bad?
big_questions.hint: Think about what is drying, and what happens inside it.

big_questions.q: Covering a canal saves water for a town. Evaporation from that canal would have become rain somewhere else. Whose water is it?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the vapour goes, and whether anyone can say where it will fall.

story.title: The Pot That Dried Too Fast
story.note: Yazhini, Ponni Paatti and their shed are made up. The science of drying clay is real. Wet clay shrinks as its water evaporates. Water leaves only from the surface, so the outside and the thin rim dry and shrink first. If they shrink much faster than the wet clay inside, the pot cracks. Potters in many parts of India dry their pots slowly in shade and out of the wind. They often cover them with damp cloth, and they turn them. A dry, unbaked pot can be soaked in water and turned back into soft clay.
text: Ponni Paatti made water pots in a tiled shed in Villianur, a short bus ride from Puducherry. In the summer holidays her granddaughter Yazhini, who was ten, came to stay and to get clay under her fingernails.

That May the heat was fierce, and a marriage hall had ordered thirty pots for its drinking water. "In six days," Paatti said. "One day for the kiln, one day to cool. So the pots have four days to dry."

By Monday noon thirty pots stood in rows at the back of the shed, dark and wet and smelling of rain. Paatti hung damp gunny sacks across the open side of the shed. She laid a strip of wet cloth round every rim.
"Paatti, that is backwards," said Yazhini. "You want them dry. Why are you making them wet?"

"Watch them for four days and tell me," said Paatti. Then her phone rang. Her sister in Cuddalore had fallen and hurt her knee. Paatti packed a bag. "I will be back on Wednesday evening. Sarasu akka next door will give you your meals. Leave the pots exactly where they are."

Yazhini meant to. But on Tuesday morning she pressed a finger on a pot, and it was as cold and damp as the day before. Four days! At home in Tiruchi she hung the washing every evening. She knew what dried a shirt: hot sun, a good wind, and plenty of room. The shed had none of the three.

So she carried six pots, one at a time, into the middle of the yard. She took the wet cloths off their rims. The sun stood overhead, and a hot west wind was blowing. By four o'clock the six pots had turned from dark brown to pale grey. She knocked on one with her knuckle. It felt hard. She was so pleased that she carried them back in and set them in the front row for Paatti to see.

On Wednesday morning she looked at the front row, and her stomach turned over. A thin line ran down from the rim of the first pot, like a hair. The second had two. The third had split right across its base.
Paatti came home at dusk. She looked at the six pots for a long time. She did not shout. She picked up the third pot and handed Yazhini a knife. "Cut through the wall and tell me what you see."
Yazhini sawed through the clay. The outside of the wall was pale and hard, like a biscuit. The middle of the wall was still dark, and it felt cool and damp on her thumb.
"Two colours," she said. "It is dry outside and wet inside."
"Where does the water leave a pot from?" Paatti asked.
Yazhini thought of her shirts. "From the outside. From where it touches the air."

"Only from there. The water in the middle of the wall has to creep out to the skin first, and that is slow. Now, clay shrinks when its water goes. Measure a wet pot and a dry pot, and the dry one is a finger narrower. Your sun and your wind took the water from the skin in one afternoon. So the skin shrank. The inside was still wet and still fat."
"A small shirt on a big body," said Yazhini slowly. "It tore."
"It tore at the rim first, because the rim is thin and has air on both sides." Paatti put the pot down. "So. Why do I hang wet sacks?"

Yazhini looked round the shed as if she had never seen it. The roof kept off the sun. The walls kept off the wind. The sacks made the air damp. The cloths covered the rims. "Everything that dries a shirt fast, you take away," she said. "You are not drying them slowly because you are slow. You hold the outside back, so that the inside can keep up."
"Then you know my whole trade," said Paatti, and she went to wash her feet.

On Thursday Paatti had to fetch firewood for the kiln. At noon the west wind rose again, hotter than before, and blew straight in at the open side. The gunny sacks had dried stiff. Yazhini saw the rims of the back rows beginning to turn pale, while the bellies of the pots were still dark.

She did not wait. She dragged the sacks down, soaked them in the trough and hung them up again, dripping. She splashed water over the earth floor. She wet the rim cloths and laid them back. Then she gave every pot a quarter turn, so that the side facing the wind became the side facing the wall.
When Paatti came back with the cart, the shed smelt of rain again. She put her palm on a rim and then on a belly, and nodded.
By Friday evening the twenty-four pots were one even grey from lip to base. Paatti rapped one, and it rang.
"Now they have finished shrinking," she said. "Now you may give them all the sun you like." Together they carried the pots out into the yard to bake dry before the kiln.
The six cracked pots went into the soaking pit. By Sunday they had slumped into soft brown clay again. Yazhini pushed her hands into it, up to the wrists.
"Six more pots," she said. "And this time I will dry them like a potter."
story.epiphany: For the parent: water evaporates only from a surface that touches the air. Sun, wind, dry air and a large exposed surface all speed this up. Clay shrinks as it loses water. So a pot dried fast shrinks on the outside while the inside is still wet and full-sized, and it cracks. Yazhini knew what makes washing dry quickly. The turn comes when she sees that her grandmother removes each of those things on purpose: shade for the sun, walls for the wind, wet sacks for the dry air, cloths over the thin rims. To slow evaporation, you need to know exactly what speeds it up.
ask: Which three things did Yazhini know would dry a shirt quickly?
The cut wall of the cracked pot had two colours. What did that show about where water leaves a pot?
Why did the rims crack first?
On Thursday Yazhini did four things in the shed. For each one, say which cause of fast evaporation it worked against.
At the end, the pots were put in full sun. Why was that safe then, and not on Tuesday?

games.title: Which Dries First? A pair card game
games.context: This is a card game about what speeds up evaporation. Each card shows two wet things. You say which will dry first, and name the reason. The answer is on the back.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A wet bedsheet hung open on a line, or the same sheet left in a heap in a bucket?
items.b: The open sheet. Bigger surface: far more of its water touches the air.

items.f: A wet shirt on a terrace at noon, or the same shirt on the terrace at night?
items.b: At noon. Warmer: the particles move faster, so more of them escape.

items.f: A wet towel under a ceiling fan, or the same towel in a room with the fan off?
items.b: Under the fan. Moving air: it carries the escaped particles away.

items.f: A swimming costume on a line in Jaipur in May, or in Mumbai in July?
items.b: In Jaipur. Drier air: fewer particles land back on the cloth.

items.f: Spilled water wiped thin across the floor, or the same water left as a puddle?
items.b: Wiped thin. Bigger surface: more particles are at the surface.

items.f: Wet hair left loose, or the same wet hair in a tight plait?
items.b: Loose hair. Bigger surface: a plait hides most of the hair inside.

items.f: Red chillies spread one deep on a mat, or the same chillies in a sack?
items.b: On the mat. Bigger surface: every chilli touches the air.

items.f: A wet umbrella left open in the veranda, or folded and strapped shut?
items.b: The open one. Bigger surface: the folds no longer cover each other.

items.f: A mopped floor on a breezy day with the windows open, or with the windows shut?
items.b: Windows open. Moving air: the breeze carries the vapour out.

items.f: A steel plate rinsed in hot water, or the same plate rinsed in cold water?
items.b: The hot one. Warmer: the film of water on it evaporates in a minute.

items.f: Clothes on a line on a misty morning after rain, or on a clear, dry morning?
items.b: The clear morning. Drier air: the misty air is already full of vapour.

items.f: A towel hung in the bathroom just after a bath, or the same towel on the balcony?
items.b: On the balcony. Drier air: bathroom air is nearly saturated after a bath.

items.f: Ink in an open bottle, or ink in a bottle with the cap on?
items.b: The open bottle. In the capped one, as many particles land back as leave.

items.f: Water in a wide, shallow uruli, or the same water in a narrow jug?
items.b: In the uruli. Bigger surface: more particles can leave each second.

items.f: Sweat on your arm on a windy beach in Chennai, or in a closed, crowded bus?
items.b: On the beach. Moving air: the wind carries the vapour away.

items.f: Raw mango cut into slices for pickle, or a whole raw mango, both in the sun?
items.b: The slices. Bigger surface: cutting opens up new surfaces.

items.f: A puddle on a tar road in the sun, or a puddle of the same size in the shade?
items.b: In the sun. Warmer: sunlight gives the particles more energy.

items.f: Fresh paint on a wall on a dry winter day in Delhi, or on a rainy day in Kochi?
items.b: In Delhi. Drier air: few particles land back on the paint.

items.f: Which mists over first: a steel tumbler of iced water, or a steel tumbler of tap water?
items.b: The iced one. Vapour particles slow down and stick only on a surface that is cold enough.

items.f: Which gets wetter: a cold bottle from the fridge in a steamy kitchen, or in an air-conditioned room?
items.b: In the steamy kitchen. More vapour in the air means more particles to condense.

printables.title: 4 reason cards to lay on the table
items: WARMER: the particles move faster, so more escape.
BIGGER SURFACE: more particles are at the surface.
MOVING AIR: escaped particles are carried away.
DRIER AIR: fewer particles land back.

rules: Lay the 4 reason cards in a row. Shuffle the 20 pair cards and put them in a pile, question side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say which of the two dries first. Then point to the reason card that explains it.
Turn the card over. If your choice and your reason are both right, keep the card.
If either is wrong, read the answer aloud and put the card at the bottom of the pile.
Two of the cards are about condensation. They ask which thing gets wet first. Answer those in your own words, without a reason card.
The game ends when the pile is gone. With friends, the player with the most cards wins. Alone, count how many cards you won on the first try.

setup.caption: 1. Lay out the 4 reason cards and the pile of pair cards.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud and pointing at the reason card that says BIGGER SURFACE.
setup.caption: 2. Say which dries first, and point to the reason.

setup.art: The card turned over to show the answer, and a small stack of won cards beside the child.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Keep it if both were right.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Lay the 4 reason cards in a row. 3. Shuffle the pair cards and pile them question side up. 4. Read the four reasons aloud together.
flow.say: Four things speed up evaporation. Read me the four reasons. Each card will ask which of two things dries first, and why.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Lay the 4 reason cards in a row. Pile up the pair cards. Read the four reasons aloud.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Dries First? Here you set out the reason cards and the pile of pair cards.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. 2. Read the top card, choose, and point to a reason. 3. Turn the card over to check. 4. Keep it if both were right. Otherwise put it at the bottom. 5. Play until the pile is gone.
flow.say: Which of these two dries first? Now point to the reason. What are the particles doing differently?
flow.kid: Read the top card. Say which dries first. Point to the reason. Turn the card over. Keep it if you were right.
flow.parent: Some cards have two good reasons. A towel on a balcony has drier air and moving air. Accept either, if your child can say what the particles do.
flow.context: This is the main part of Which Dries First? Here you take turns to say which of two wet things dries first, and why.

flow.do: 1. Each player sorts the cards they won under the four reason cards. 2. Ask which reason came up most. 3. Ask your child to make up one new card from your own home.
flow.say: Sort your cards by reason. Which reason came up most? Now make up a new card from our home.
flow.kid: Sort your cards under the four reasons. Which pile is biggest? Make up one new card of your own.

check.q: Two wet shirts hang side by side in the same breeze. One is in the sun and one in the shade. Which reason explains why the sunny one dries first?
options: Warmer: its particles move faster
Bigger surface: it is spread wider
Drier air: the sun removes vapour
check.why: Both shirts have the same surface and the same breeze. Sunlight gives the water particles more energy, so more of them are fast enough to escape.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Dries First? Here you sort the cards you won by reason, and make up a new card.

games.title: Fast Ones Leave: a dice game about cooling
games.context: This is a dice game about why evaporation cools water. Twelve squares stand for twelve particles of water, and a die gives each one a speed. The fastest particles at the surface escape, and you watch what happens to the average speed.

printables.title: A pot to draw: 3 rows of 4 squares
items: Draw a rectangle with 3 rows of 4 squares, each square about 3 cm wide. This is the pot.
Each square is one particle of water. Leave room in each square for a number.
Write ROUND 1 beside the top row, ROUND 2 beside the middle row and ROUND 3 beside the bottom row.
Draw a cloud shape above the pot and write AIR in it.

printables.title: A score sheet
items: My guess: will the average go up, go down or stay the same?
Start: 12 particles. Total of the speeds: ___. Average: ___.
After round 1: particles left ___. Total ___. Average ___.
After round 2: particles left ___. Total ___. Average ___.
After round 3: particles left ___. Total ___. Average ___.
After the Sun round: particles left ___. Total ___. Average ___.

rules: You need the pot drawn on paper, a pencil, a score sheet and one die.
Roll the die once for each of the 12 squares, and write the number in the square. The number is that particle's speed.
Add up the 12 speeds and divide by 12. This average stands for the temperature of your pot. Write it on the score sheet.
The water stirs itself, so each row takes a turn at the surface. In round 1 the top row is at the surface. In round 2 it is the middle row, and in round 3 the bottom row.
In each round, every particle in the surface row with a speed of 5 or 6 escapes. Cross out its square and write its speed in the AIR cloud.
After each round, add up the speeds still in the pot. Divide by the number of particles left. Write the new average, to one decimal place.
Then play the Sun round. Add 1 to every speed still in the pot. Now any particle with a speed of 5 escapes. Work out the last average.

With friends, each player has a pot and plays the three rounds. The coolest pot, with the lowest average after round 3, wins. Alone, guess your round 3 average before you roll, and see how close you get.

setup.art: A hand-drawn pot of twelve squares in three rows, each square holding a number from 1 to 6, with a die beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Roll the die 12 times and write a speed in each square.

setup.art: The same pot with two squares in the top row crossed out and the numbers 6 and 5 written in a cloud above.
setup.caption: 2. In the surface row, every 5 and 6 escapes into the AIR cloud.

setup.art: A score sheet beside the pot with four averages written in a column, each smaller than the one above.
setup.caption: 3. Work out the average of the particles left after each round.

flow.do: 1. Draw the pot and the AIR cloud. 2. Roll the die 12 times and write a speed in each square. 3. Add up the speeds and divide by 12. 4. Ask what will happen to the average when the fastest particles leave, and why.
flow.say: Each number is the speed of one particle. The average is the temperature of the pot. When the fast ones at the surface leave, what will happen to the average? Why?
flow.kid: Draw the pot. Roll the die 12 times. Write a speed in each square. Find the average. Guess what will happen to it.
flow.parent: A phone calculator is fine for the division. For example, a total of 42 gives 42 ÷ 12 = 3.5.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fast Ones Leave. Here you give twelve particles of water their speeds with a die, and find their average speed.

flow.do: 1. Play round 1. Cross out every 5 and 6 in the top row and write them in the AIR cloud. 2. Work out the new average. 3. Play round 2 with the middle row and round 3 with the bottom row. 4. Write the average after each round.
flow.say: Which particles escaped? Look at the ones left behind. Is the pot warmer or cooler than before? Did the average ever go up?
flow.kid: Cross out each 5 and 6 in the top row. Find the new average. Do the middle row next, then the bottom row.
flow.parent: The average falls whenever a particle leaves, and it never rises. After three rounds it is usually between 2 and 3. If no 5 or 6 is in a row, nothing leaves in that round.
flow.context: This is the main part of Fast Ones Leave. Here the fastest particles in each surface row escape, and you work out the average speed of the particles left.

flow.do: 1. Play the Sun round. Add 1 to every speed still in the pot. 2. Cross out every particle that now has a speed of 5. 3. Work out the last average. 4. Ask what the Sun round shows about warm water.
flow.say: The Sun has warmed the pot, and every particle is faster by 1. How many more escaped? What does that tell you about warm water and evaporation?
flow.kid: Add 1 to every speed left in the pot. Cross out each 5. How many escaped this time? Find the last average.

ask.q: Why did the average fall each time particles left?
good: Only the fastest ones left, so the ones left behind were slower on average.

ask.q: What did the Sun round show?
good: Warming makes more particles fast enough to escape, so warm water evaporates faster.

check.q: In Fast Ones Leave, the average speed fell whenever particles escaped. What does this show about real water?
options: Evaporation cools the water left behind
Evaporation heats the water left behind
All water particles have the same speed
check.why: The particles that escape are the fastest ones. The average of the rest is lower, and a lower average speed means a lower temperature. If all particles had the same speed, the average could not change.

flow.context: This is the last step of Fast Ones Leave. Here the Sun warms the pot, so every particle speeds up, and you see how many more can escape.

experiments.title: Wide or Narrow: does a bigger surface lose more water?
experiments.context: This experiment takes two days. You put the same amount of water into a wide plate, a bowl, a tumbler and a closed jar. A day later you measure how much water each has lost. Then you compare the loss with the size of each water surface.
experiments.question: The same amount of water stands in a wide plate, a bowl and a tumbler for one day. Which loses the most? If one surface is 4 times as big as another, does it lose 4 times as much water?
experiments.predict: Guess first, and write your guesses. Put the plate, the bowl, the tumbler and the closed jar in order. Start with the one that will lose the most water. Then guess a number. A plate twice as wide as a bowl has about 4 times the surface. How many times as much water will the plate lose? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Put the same amount of water in every vessel, measured in the same glass. Stand all four side by side, in the same room, under the same fan, out of the sun. Measure them all after the same time. Only the size of the water surface is different. The closed jar shows how much water is lost just by pouring.
results_table: Height in the measuring glass at the start (mm)

materials.item: a clear glass or jar with straight sides, to measure with
a ruler marked in millimetres
a steel plate with a rim, about 20 cm across
a steel bowl, about 10 cm across
a steel tumbler
a jar with a screw lid, such as a pickle or jam jar
tap water
a big bowl to pour over, a pencil and paper

schedule.what: Guess. Measure the same amount of water into the plate, the bowl, the tumbler and the jar. Close the jar. Measure each water surface and work out its area.
Pour each vessel's water back into the measuring glass and read the height. Work out the loss, compare it with the area, and explain.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each vessel, showing the height lost. Then write what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: water lost in one day

example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A clear straight-sided glass of water with a ruler held upright against it, the water level at the 50 mm mark.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the measuring glass to 50 mm.

setup.art: A steel plate, a steel bowl, a steel tumbler and a closed jar in a row on a table under a ceiling fan, each holding water.
setup.caption: 2. Pour 50 mm of water into each vessel. Close the jar. Leave them side by side.

flow.do: 1. Stand the measuring glass on the table. 2. Hold the ruler upright against it, with the zero at the level of the inside of the bottom. 3. Pour in water until the top of the water is at 50 mm. 4. Show your child how to read the height with an eye level with the water.
flow.say: This glass is our measuring glass. We will give every vessel exactly this much water, 50 millimetres in the glass. Why must every vessel get the same amount?
flow.kid: Hold the ruler against the glass. Pour in water up to 50 millimetres. Read it with your eye level with the water.
flow.parent: Any clear vessel with straight sides works. In a glass about 6 cm across, 50 mm is about 150 millilitres.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wide or Narrow. Here you learn to measure the same amount of water each time. The amount is a height of 50 mm in one glass.

flow.do: 1. Show the plate, the bowl, the tumbler and the jar with its lid. 2. Ask your child to put them in order, from the most water lost in a day to the least. 3. Ask how many times as much the plate will lose as the bowl. 4. Write both guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: All four will get the same water and stand in the same place for a day. Which will lose the most? How many times as much as the bowl? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which vessel will lose the most water in a day. Put all four in order. Say why. Write it down.

good: The plate, because its water is spread out.
The tumbler, because it is small.
They will all lose the same, because they hold the same water.

flow.context: This step of Wide or Narrow is for guessing. You guess which of four vessels will lose the most water in one day, and by how much.

flow.do: 1. Put the four vessels side by side, under the fan and out of the sun. 2. Pour the 50 mm of water from the glass into the plate. 3. Fill the glass to 50 mm again for the bowl, again for the tumbler and again for the jar. 4. Screw the lid on the jar. 5. Write down the time.
flow.say: Pour slowly, so that no water spills. Now the only thing that differs is the shape. Which part of the water touches the air in each one?
flow.kid: Pour 50 millimetres of water into each vessel. Close the jar. Put all four side by side. Write the time.
flow.parent: Put the plate in its place before you fill it, because a full plate is hard to carry. Keep all four where nobody will knock them.
flow.context: This step of Wide or Narrow sets up the test. You put the same amount of water in a plate, a bowl, a tumbler and a closed jar.

flow.do: 1. Lay the ruler across each water surface and read its width in centimetres. 2. Work out each area. Multiply the width by itself, then take three-quarters of the answer. 3. Write the widths and the areas in the table.
flow.say: A circle fills about three-quarters of the square drawn round it. So multiply the width by itself, and take three-quarters. How many times as big is the plate's surface as the bowl's?
flow.kid: Measure across the water in each vessel. Multiply the width by itself. Take three-quarters. That is the area.
flow.parent: For a width of 20 cm: 20 × 20 = 400, and three-quarters of 400 is 300 square cm. For 10 cm: 100, then 75. For 7 cm: 49, then about 37. Measure the water surface, which in a plate is a little smaller than the rim.
flow.wait: Leave the four vessels for one day
flow.context: This step of Wide or Narrow measures the size of each water surface. You find the area of a circle from its width.

flow.do: 1. After about one day, stand the measuring glass in the big bowl. 2. Pour the jar's water into the glass and read the height. 3. Empty the glass, then do the same for the tumbler, the bowl and the plate. 4. For each, take the new height away from 50 mm. That is the height lost.
flow.say: Read each height carefully. Which vessel lost the most? Did the closed jar lose any?
flow.kid: Pour each vessel's water back into the glass. Read the height. Take it away from 50. Write what each one lost.
flow.parent: If any water spills into the big bowl, tip it into the glass before you read. Under a fan in dry weather the plate may lose 20 to 40 mm. On a humid day it may lose about 10 mm. Then you can leave the test for a second day. If the jar reads 1 mm low, that water was left behind in pouring. Take 1 mm off the other losses too.
flow.context: This step of Wide or Narrow is done one day later. You pour each vessel's water back into the measuring glass to find how much each has lost.

flow.do: 1. Look at the areas and the losses side by side. 2. Ask how many times as big the plate's surface is as the bowl's. 3. Ask how many times as much water the plate lost. 4. Do the same for the bowl and the tumbler. 5. Draw the bar chart.
flow.say: How many times as big is the plate's surface as the bowl's? About how many times as much water did it lose? Did the tumbler lose as much as its surface suggests?
flow.kid: Compare the plate with the bowl. How many times bigger is its surface? How many times more water did it lose?
flow.parent: The plate usually loses about 4 times as much as the bowl. The tumbler often loses less than its area suggests. Its walls stand above the water and shelter it from the fan, so damp air collects there.
flow.context: This step of Wide or Narrow compares the water lost by each vessel with the size of its water surface.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 2. After they have answered, read them the note below. 3. Ask why the closed jar lost nothing.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then tell me this: the jar had the same water. Why did it lose none?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened. Why did the closed jar lose no water?

ask.q: Why did the plate lose the most?
good: It had the biggest surface, so the most particles were at the surface and could leave.

ask.q: Why did the closed jar lose none?
good: Particles still left the water, but they could not get away. As many landed back as left.

flow.parent: Water leaves only from its surface. A surface 4 times as big has about 4 times as many particles on it. So about 4 times as many escape each second. In the closed jar the air soon became saturated. Then as many particles landed back on the water as left it.
flow.think: A lake and a puddle stand in the same sunshine. Which loses more water in a day? Which loses more depth?

check.q: In Wide or Narrow, the plate had 4 times the bowl's surface. It lost about 4 times as much water. What does this show?
options: Water leaves only from its surface
A plate holds more water than a bowl
Steel plates pull water out
check.why: Both held the same amount of water, so the amount did not decide it. The loss grew in step with the surface, because only particles at the surface can escape. Both vessels were steel, so the material was the same.

flow.context: This is the last step of Wide or Narrow. Here you explain why the plate lost the most water and the closed jar lost none.

experiments.title: The Oil Lid: does water cool more slowly when it cannot evaporate?
experiments.context: In this experiment two bowls hold the same hot water. A thin layer of cooking oil covers the water in one bowl, so that no water can evaporate from it. You find out which bowl cools faster.
experiments.question: Two bowls of hot water start at the same temperature. One has a layer of oil on top, which stops the water evaporating. Does it cool as fast as the open bowl?
experiments.predict: Guess first, and write your guess. After 20 minutes, which bowl will be cooler: the open one, the one under oil, or neither? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two bowls of the same size and the same steel. Give each the same amount of water from the same jug, at the same moment. Stand them side by side, away from the fan. The only difference is the layer of oil.
results_table: Open bowl: how warm it feels, or its temperature
Oil bowl: how warm it feels, or its temperature

materials.item: small steel bowls of the same size, about 10 cm across
hot water: one tumbler of boiling water mixed with two tumblers of tap water in a steel jug
cooking oil
a tablespoon
a cold, dry steel plate
a clock
a thermometer that reads up to 60 degrees Celsius, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils, mixes and pours the water, and holds the plate. The water is hot, like bath water from a geyser. Touch only the outside of the bowls, and only after the grown-up has tested them.

schedule.what: Guess. Pour hot water into two bowls and cover one with oil. Test for vapour with a cold plate. Feel both bowls after 10 and 20 minutes, and explain.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. If you used a thermometer, draw a line graph with two lines, one for each bowl. Then write what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: two bowls of hot water cooling (degrees Celsius)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Two small steel bowls side by side on a kitchen counter, each being filled with steaming water from a steel jug.
setup.caption: 1. Pour the same hot water into two bowls of the same size.

setup.art: A tablespoon of oil being poured gently over the back of a second spoon onto the water in one bowl, with a golden layer spreading across it.
setup.caption: 2. Float 2 tablespoons of oil on one bowl, so that it covers all the water.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a cold steel plate just above the open bowl, with mist forming on its underside.
setup.caption: 3. Hold a cold plate above each bowl. Which one mists the plate?

setup.art: A child touching the outsides of both bowls at once, one with each hand, with a clock behind.
setup.caption: 4. After 10 and 20 minutes, feel which bowl is cooler.

flow.do: 1. Show the two bowls, the jug and the oil. 2. Say that the oil will float and cover the water in one bowl, so no water can evaporate from it. 3. Ask which bowl will be cooler after 20 minutes, and why. 4. Write the guess.
flow.say: Both bowls get the same hot water. One gets a lid of oil, so its water cannot evaporate. After 20 minutes, which will be cooler? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two bowls get the same hot water. One gets oil on top. Guess which will be cooler in 20 minutes. Say why.

good: The open bowl, because heat leaves with the vapour.
The same, because both lose heat through the steel.
The oil bowl, because oil is cold.

flow.context: This is the first step of The Oil Lid. Here you guess whether hot water under oil cools as fast as hot water in an open bowl.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up mixes one tumbler of boiling water with two tumblers of tap water in the jug. 2. Pour one tumbler of this water into each bowl. 3. Pour 2 tablespoons of oil gently over the back of a spoon onto bowl B. 4. Check that the oil covers the whole surface. If there is a gap, add a third spoonful. 5. Note the time.
flow.say: Watch the oil spread. Is any water still open to the air in bowl B? Now both bowls are equally hot. Only the oil is different.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours hot water into both bowls. Oil goes on one bowl. Check that the oil covers all the water.
flow.parent: Oil does not mix with water, and it floats. It hardly evaporates at all. So it works as a lid that touches the water everywhere. If you have a thermometer, read both bowls now.
flow.context: This step of The Oil Lid sets up the test. A grown-up pours the same hot water into two bowls and floats a layer of oil on one of them.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up holds the cold, dry plate about 5 cm above bowl A for 10 seconds. 2. Look at the underside of the plate. 3. Wipe the plate dry. 4. Do the same above bowl B.
flow.say: Look under the plate each time. Above which bowl did it turn misty? What does the mist tell you is leaving that bowl?
flow.kid: A grown-up holds a cold plate above each bowl. Look under the plate. Which bowl made it misty?
flow.parent: The plate mists above the open bowl and stays almost clear above the oil. So vapour is leaving bowl A and not bowl B.
flow.context: This step of The Oil Lid tests which bowl is giving off water vapour. A cold plate is held above each bowl in turn.

flow.do: 1. Wait until 10 minutes have passed since the pouring. 2. The grown-up touches the outside of each bowl first. 3. Your child puts one hand on each bowl, then swaps hands. 4. Write which bowl feels cooler. 5. With a thermometer, read both bowls every 5 minutes.
flow.say: Put one hand on each bowl. Now swap your hands. Which bowl is cooler? Is it a small difference or a big one?
flow.kid: Wait 10 minutes. Put one hand on each bowl. Swap hands. Which bowl feels cooler? Write it down.
flow.parent: Swapping hands matters. A hand that has just held something warm judges the next thing as cooler. While you wait, your child can draw the two bowls.
flow.context: This step of The Oil Lid is the first check, 10 minutes after pouring. You feel which of the two bowls of hot water has cooled more.

flow.do: 1. At 20 minutes, feel both bowls again, and swap hands. 2. Write which is cooler now. 3. With a thermometer, take the last reading and work out the difference.
flow.say: Twenty minutes have passed. Which bowl is cooler now? Has the difference grown?
flow.kid: At 20 minutes, feel both bowls again. Swap hands. Which is cooler now? Has the difference grown?
flow.parent: The open bowl is usually clearly cooler. With a thermometer the gap is often 4 to 8 degrees. When the bowls are cold, skim off the oil and use it in a lamp.
flow.context: This step of The Oil Lid is the second check, 20 minutes after pouring. You feel the two bowls again and see whether the difference has grown.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 2. After they have answered, read them the note below. 3. Ask what the cold plate showed.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Both bowls lost heat through the steel. What else was the open bowl losing?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened. What did the cold plate show?

ask.q: Both bowls lost heat through the steel. What else was the open bowl losing?
good: Water vapour. The plate misted above it.
Its fastest particles, which escaped from the surface.

flow.parent: The particles of the hot water move at many different speeds. In the open bowl the fastest ones at the surface kept escaping. The particles left behind were slower on average, and slower particles mean cooler water. Under the oil no particle could escape, so that bowl lost heat only through the steel and the oil.
flow.think: Why does a thin skin of cream on hot milk keep the milk hot for longer?

check.q: In The Oil Lid, the open bowl cooled faster than the bowl under oil. Why?
options: Its fastest particles kept escaping
The oil made the other bowl hotter
Open water takes in cold from the air
check.why: Evaporation removes the fastest particles, so the water left behind is cooler. The oil added no heat. It only stopped particles leaving. Cold does not flow into the water from the air. What happens is that heat flows out of the water, and the escaping particles carry heat away.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Oil Lid. Here you explain why the open bowl of hot water cooled faster than the bowl sealed with oil.

experiments.title: The Tilting Hanger: spread, fan or sunshine, which dries a cloth fastest?
experiments.context: In this experiment a coat hanger is a balance. Two wet cloths that weigh the same are dried in two different ways for 8 minutes. Then the hanger shows which cloth has lost more water.
experiments.question: Three things can speed up drying: spreading the cloth out, moving air and warmth. In your home today, which of the three makes the biggest difference in 8 minutes?
experiments.predict: Guess first, and write your guess. You will run three tests. The first is a spread cloth against a folded cloth. The second is a cloth under the fan against a cloth in still air. The third is a test that you choose. In which test will the two cloths end up most different? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Start each test with two cloths that balance on the hanger, so they hold the same water. In each test change only one thing. In the first test both cloths are under the fan, and only the folding differs. In the second both are spread out, and only the moving air differs. Give both cloths the same 8 minutes.
results_table: How many centimetres did its end rise?

materials.item: a coat hanger, and a door handle or hook to hang it from
clothes clips
cotton handkerchiefs of the same kind, or two equal squares cut from an old cotton cloth
a bowl of water and a teaspoon
a sheet of paper, sticky tape, a pencil and a ruler
a ceiling fan or table fan
a chair, a plate and a clock

schedule.what: Make a hanger balance. Run three 8-minute drying tests with two wet cloths, measure which cloth lost more water each time, and explain.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each test, showing how far the lighter cloth's end rose. Then write what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how far the drier cloth's end rose
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A coat hanger hanging from a door handle with a clothes clip at each end, and a sheet of paper taped behind one end with a pencil mark.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a hanger with a clip at each end. Mark where one end sits.

setup.art: Two wet handkerchiefs, each bunched and held by a clip at one end of the hanger, with the hanger level.
setup.caption: 2. Clip on two wet cloths and make them balance.

setup.art: One wet handkerchief spread open over the back of a chair and the other folded small on a plate on the seat, under a ceiling fan.
setup.caption: 3. Dry them in two different ways for 8 minutes.

setup.art: The two cloths back on the hanger, one end clearly higher, with a ruler held upright beside the pencil mark.
setup.caption: 4. Clip them back on. Measure how far the lighter end has risen.

flow.do: 1. Hang the coat hanger on a door handle or hook, away from the fan. 2. Fix one clothes clip to each end. 3. If one end is lower, stick bits of tape on the higher end until the hanger is level. 4. Tape the paper behind one end and mark where that end sits.
flow.say: This hanger is our balance. If two cloths hold the same water, it sits level. If one has lost more water, which way will it tilt?
flow.kid: Hang the hanger on a door handle. Put a clip on each end. Make it level with tape. Mark where one end sits.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Tilting Hanger. Here you turn a coat hanger into a balance and mark where it sits when it is level.

flow.do: 1. Dip both cloths in the bowl. 2. Hold them together and squeeze until the dripping stops. 3. Bunch each cloth and clip one to each end of the hanger. 4. If one end is lower, drip water from the teaspoon onto the other cloth until the hanger is level. 5. Ask for the guess and its reason.
flow.say: Now the two cloths hold the same water. We will dry them in different ways. In which of our three tests will they end up most different? Why?
flow.kid: Wet both cloths. Squeeze them together. Clip one to each end. Add drops until the hanger is level. Now guess.

good: Spreading, because a folded cloth hides most of its surface.
The fan, because moving air carries the vapour away.
The sun, because warmth makes the particles faster.

flow.context: This step of The Tilting Hanger makes the start fair. You wet two cloths and balance them on the hanger, so both hold the same amount of water.

flow.do: 1. Take both cloths off. 2. Spread cloth A open over the back of a chair, under the fan. 3. Fold cloth B in four and lay it on a plate on the seat of the same chair. 4. Wait 8 minutes. 5. Clip both back on the hanger. Measure how far the lighter cloth's end has risen above the mark.
flow.say: Both cloths were under the same fan. Only the folding was different. Which end rose? How many centimetres?
flow.kid: Spread one cloth on a chair back. Fold the other in four on a plate. Wait 8 minutes. Clip them back on. Which end rose?
flow.parent: The spread cloth is lighter, often by a few grams, and its end rises 1 to 4 cm. If the mark is on the other end, measure how far that end has dropped. It is the same distance.
flow.context: This step of The Tilting Hanger is the first test. One wet cloth is spread out and the other is folded in four. Both are dried under the same fan.

flow.do: 1. Wet both cloths again and balance them as before. 2. Spread cloth A over the chair under the fan. 3. Spread cloth B over another chair in a room with the fan off. 4. Wait 8 minutes. 5. Clip both back on and measure the rise.
flow.say: This time both cloths are spread out. Only the moving air is different. Which end rose, and how far?
flow.kid: Wet and balance the cloths again. Spread one under the fan. Spread one in still air. Wait 8 minutes. Measure again.
flow.parent: Choose a still room that is about as warm as the room with the fan. Do not use the bathroom, because its air is damp.
flow.context: This step of The Tilting Hanger is the second test. Both wet cloths are spread out, one under a fan and one in still air.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to plan a third test that changes one new thing. It could be a sunny spot against a shady one, or a bathroom after a bath against a bedroom. 2. They say what will differ and what will stay the same. 3. Wet and balance the cloths, run the test for 8 minutes, and measure.
flow.say: Now plan your own test. What one thing will you change? What must stay the same for both cloths?
flow.kid: Plan your own test. Change one thing only. Say what stays the same. Run it for 8 minutes. Measure the rise.
flow.parent: If your child wants to change two things at once, ask how they would know which one made the difference.
flow.context: This step of The Tilting Hanger is a third test that you plan yourself. You choose one new thing to change, such as sunshine or damp air.

flow.do: 1. Put the three results side by side and draw the bar chart. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Which change made the biggest difference in our home today?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened. Which change mattered most today?

good: Spread out: more of the water is at a surface, so more particles can leave.
Fan: moving air carries escaped particles away, so fewer land back.
Sun: warm particles move faster, so more of them can escape.

flow.parent: The order changes from home to home and from day to day. On a humid day the fan may matter most. On a dry, hot day spreading may matter most. All three work by letting more particles leave than land back.
flow.think: Would the order of your three results be the same in the monsoon as in May? How could you find out?

check.q: In The Tilting Hanger, a cloth under a fan lost more water than the same cloth in still air. Why does moving air speed up evaporation?
options: It carries escaped particles away
It makes the water hotter
It pushes water out of the cloth
check.why: In still air the escaped particles collect near the cloth, and many land back on it. Moving air sweeps them away. A fan does not heat the water. It usually cools a wet cloth a little.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Tilting Hanger. Here you compare three drying tests and explain each result with particles.

activities.title: Tumbler or Davara: which cools hot water faster?
activities.context: This is the first thing to do in the unit. A grown-up pours the same hot water into a tumbler and into a wide davara. You find out which one cools faster, and wonder why.

materials.item: a steel tumbler
a davara, or a wide steel bowl or a plate with a rim
hot water: one tumbler of boiling water mixed with two tumblers of tap water
a steel jug and a clock

activities.safety: A grown-up boils, mixes and pours the water. The mixed water is hot, like bath water from a geyser. Touch only the outside of the vessels, and only after the grown-up has tested them.
