activities.record: Draw the tumbler and the davara from above. Shade the water surface of each. Write which one cooled faster.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring steaming water from a steel jug into a steel tumbler, with a wide davara beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Pour the same amount of hot water into a tumbler and a davara.

setup.art: A child holding one palm above the tumbler and then above the davara, with a clock on the counter.
setup.caption: 2. Wait 4 minutes. Feel the air above each one.

setup.art: A child touching the outside of the tumbler with one hand and the davara with the other.
setup.caption: 3. Touch the outsides. Which is cooler?

flow.do: 1. A grown-up mixes one tumbler of boiling water with two tumblers of tap water in a jug. 2. Pour half a tumbler of this water into the steel tumbler. 3. Pour the same amount into the davara. 4. Ask your child which will be cooler after 4 minutes, and why. 5. Note the time.
flow.say: Both hold the same hot water. In four minutes, which will be cooler, the tumbler or the davara? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A grown-up pours hot water into a tumbler and a davara. Guess which will cool faster. Say why.

good: The davara, because the water is spread out.
The tumbler, because it is smaller.
They will be the same, because it is the same water.

flow.parent: Use the same amount in each, about half a tumbler. Do not explain anything yet. This activity is for noticing and wondering.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tumbler or Davara. Here a grown-up pours the same hot water into a narrow vessel and a wide one. You guess which will cool faster.

flow.do: 1. Wait 4 minutes. 2. Ask your child to hold a palm about 10 cm above each vessel in turn. 3. Ask which one sends up more warm, damp air. 4. Look for a faint mist above each.
flow.say: Hold your palm above the tumbler, and then above the davara. What do you feel on your skin? Is it the same above both?
flow.kid: Wait 4 minutes. Hold your palm above each one. Do not touch the water. What do you feel?
flow.parent: The air above the davara usually feels warmer and damper. Water vapour is leaving from the whole wide surface.
flow.context: This step of Tumbler or Davara is the wait. You feel the warm, damp air rising from the hot water in the tumbler and in the davara.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up touches the outside of each vessel first. 2. Then your child touches both, one with each hand. 3. Ask which is cooler, and what was different about the two vessels. 4. Write down what your child notices and wonders.
flow.say: Which one is cooler now? The water and the room were the same. What was different? What do you wonder about?
flow.kid: Touch the outside of each one. Which is cooler? What was different about them? What do you wonder?
flow.parent: The davara is clearly cooler. Its water has a bigger surface, so more of its fastest particles escape each second. A wide dish also loses more heat straight to the steel and to the air. The Oil Lid, a later experiment in this unit, tests evaporation alone.
flow.think: People in Tamil Nadu pour hot coffee back and forth between a davara and a tumbler. What does the pouring do to the surface of the coffee?

check.q: Hot water cooled faster in a wide davara than in a tumbler. What was different about the water in the davara?
options: It had a bigger surface touching the air
It was a different kind of water
It was colder when it was poured
check.why: The same water was poured into both, at the same temperature. Only the shape was different. The davara gave the water a bigger surface, so heat and fast particles could leave it more quickly.

flow.context: This is the last step of Tumbler or Davara. Here you feel which vessel of hot water has cooled more, and say what was different about the two.

activities.title: Shake the Plate: a model of particles leaving water
activities.context: In this activity whole chana in a steel plate stand for the particles of water. You shake the plate gently and then harder, and count how many chana jump out. It is a model of evaporation.

materials.item: a steel plate with a low rim, about 1 cm high
whole dry chana or dry peas
a bedsheet or a big tray to catch the chana
a second plate to use as a lid
a clock that shows seconds

activities.record: Make a table with three rows: gentle shake, hard shake, hard shake with a lid. Write how many chana left the plate each time.

setup.art: A steel plate holding about forty chana, standing on a bedsheet spread on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Put 40 chana in a plate on a bedsheet.

setup.art: Two hands sliding the plate quickly from side to side, with several chana flying over the rim.
setup.caption: 2. Shake gently for 10 seconds, then harder. Count the chana that jump out.

setup.art: The same plate being shaken with a second plate held upside down a little way above it.
setup.caption: 3. Shake again with a lid held above. Do the chana come back?

flow.do: 1. Spread the bedsheet on the floor. 2. Put the plate in the middle with 40 chana in it. 3. Tell your child what stands for what. Each chana is a particle of water. The rim stands for the hold that the particles have on each other. Shaking stands for warmth. 4. Ask for a guess: how many will jump out with a gentle shake, and with a hard shake?
flow.say: Each chana is a particle of water. The rim stands for the hold they have on each other. When I shake gently, how many will get out? And when I shake hard? Why?
flow.kid: Put 40 chana in the plate. Each chana is a water particle. Guess how many will jump out. Say why.

good: A hard shake makes them move faster, so more will get over the rim.
Only the ones near the edge can get out.

flow.context: This is the first step of Shake the Plate. Here you set up a plate of chana as a model of water particles. You guess how many will jump out.

flow.do: 1. Slide the plate gently from side to side on the sheet for 10 seconds. 2. Count the chana that left the plate, and write the number. 3. Put them back. 4. Shake harder for 10 seconds, without lifting the plate. 5. Count and write again.
flow.say: Watch the chana that get out. Where in the plate were they just before they left? Were they slow ones or fast ones?
flow.kid: Slide the plate gently for 10 seconds. Count the chana that jumped out. Put them back. Now shake harder. Count again.
flow.parent: A gentle shake usually loses 0 to 3 chana. A hard shake loses 8 to 20. The ones that leave are at the rim and moving fast, like the fastest particles at the surface of water.
flow.context: This is the main step of Shake the Plate. Here you shake a plate of chana gently and then harder. You count how many chana jump over the rim each time.

flow.do: 1. Put all 40 chana back. 2. One person holds the second plate upside down, about 3 cm above the first. 3. The other shakes hard for 10 seconds. 4. Count the chana that left.
flow.say: Now the plate has a lid. The chana still jump. Where do they go this time?
flow.kid: Hold a second plate just above the first. Shake hard again. How many chana got out this time?
flow.parent: Most jumpers hit the lid and fall back in. A capped bottle of water works in the same way. Particles still leave the water, but they land back, so the level stays the same.
flow.context: This step of Shake the Plate adds a lid. You see what happens to chana that jump when they cannot get away.

flow.do: 1. Look at the three numbers. 2. Ask what the model shows about real water. 3. Ask where the model is unlike real water.
flow.say: What does this model show about evaporation? And in what way is a plate of chana not like real water?
flow.kid: Look at your three numbers. What does the model show about water? How is real water different?

ask.q: How is real water different from the chana?
good: Nobody shakes real water. Its particles move by themselves all the time.
Real particles are far too small to see, and there are far more of them.
In real water, particles from the air also land back on the surface.

check.q: In Shake the Plate, which chana jumped out of the plate?
options: Fast ones that reached the rim
Slow ones in the middle
All of them, at the same moment
check.why: Only chana at the rim with enough speed got over it. Water is like this. Only fast particles at the surface escape. Choosing 'all of them' forgets that the particles have many different speeds.

flow.context: This is the last step of Shake the Plate. Here you say what the chana model shows about evaporation, and where the model is unlike real water.

activities.title: Draw the Particles: four changes of state
activities.context: In this activity you draw the particles of ice, water and water vapour. Then you join them with four arrows, one for each change of state. You show where heat goes in and where it comes out.

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper
a pencil, a red pencil and a blue pencil
a coin to draw round

activities.record: Keep the finished drawing. You use it again in Zoom In on the Water Cycle.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three boxes of the same size at the corners of a triangle, labelled ice, water and water vapour.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three boxes of the same size: ice, water and water vapour.

setup.art: The three boxes filled with small circles: neat rows, a jumbled crowd, and two far-apart circles with arrows.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the particles in each box.

setup.art: The triangle with four labelled arrows between the boxes, two coloured red and two coloured blue.
setup.caption: 3. Add four arrows. Red means heat goes in. Blue means heat comes out.

flow.do: 1. Draw three boxes of the same size at the corners of a triangle. Label them ice, water and water vapour. 2. Ask your child to draw the particles of each, all the same size. 3. Ask them to add a short arrow to each particle, to show how it moves.
flow.say: Draw the particles of ice, of water and of water vapour. Make every particle the same size. How close are they in each box? How do they move?
flow.kid: Draw three boxes. Label them ice, water and water vapour. Draw the particles in each box. Show how they move.
flow.parent: In the ice box, the particles sit in rows, touching, and they only shake in place. In the water box, the particles touch, are jumbled and slide past each other. In the vapour box, there are only one or two particles, far apart, with long arrows. If the vapour box is crowded, ask how much space steam takes.
flow.context: This is the first step of Draw the Particles. Here you draw how the particles of ice, water and water vapour are arranged and how they move.

flow.do: 1. Draw an arrow from ice to water and one from water to ice. 2. Draw an arrow from water to vapour and one from vapour to water. 3. Ask your child to name each arrow: melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation. 4. Colour an arrow red if heat must go in, and blue if heat must come out.
flow.say: Name each arrow. For which two changes must heat go in? For which two must heat come out?
flow.kid: Draw four arrows between the boxes. Name each one. Colour it red if heat goes in. Colour it blue if heat comes out.

ask.q: Which two arrows are red, and why?
good: Melting and evaporation. The particles need energy to break away from each other.

ask.q: Which pairs of arrows undo each other?
good: Melting and freezing.
Evaporation and condensation.

flow.context: This step of Draw the Particles adds the four changes of state as arrows. You colour each arrow to show whether heat goes in or comes out.

flow.do: 1. Draw a big circle below the triangle. 2. In it, ask your child to draw the surface of water with about 15 particles. 3. They give each particle a short or a long arrow. 4. They show two long-arrowed particles at the top leaving.
flow.say: Now zoom in on the surface while the water evaporates. Which particles leave? What is left behind?
flow.kid: Draw a big circle. Draw the top of the water inside it. Give some particles long arrows. Show which ones leave.

check.q: Which two changes of state happen only when heat goes into the water?
options: Melting and evaporation
Freezing and condensation
Melting and freezing
check.why: In melting and in evaporation, particles break away from their neighbours, and that takes energy. In freezing and condensation they join again and give the energy out. Melting and freezing are a pair that undo each other.

flow.context: This is the last step of Draw the Particles. Here you draw a close view of the water surface, to show which particles leave when water evaporates.

activities.title: What Is in the Bubbles? Watch water boil
activities.context: In this activity you watch a pan of water with a grown-up as it warms and then boils. You see two kinds of bubbles, and find out what is inside each kind.

materials.item: a steel pan
tap water
a stove
a cold, dry steel plate or lid, and a thick cloth to hold it

activities.safety: A grown-up works the stove and holds the plate. Children watch from an arm's length away. Steam burns badly, so nobody puts a hand or face over the pan.
activities.record: Draw the pan twice: when the water is warm, and when it is boiling. Draw the bubbles and write what is inside them.

setup.art: A steel pan of water on a low flame, with tiny bubbles clinging to the bottom and the walls.
setup.caption: 1. Warm the water. Tiny bubbles appear on the bottom and walls.

setup.art: The same pan at a full boil, with large bubbles rising from the bottom and breaking at the top.
setup.caption: 2. At the boil, big bubbles rise from the bottom.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a steel plate with a cloth high above the pan, and drops forming under the plate.
setup.caption: 3. A cold plate held high above the pan gets wet.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up puts 2 tumblers of tap water in the pan and lights the stove. 2. Watch from an arm's length. 3. After a minute or two, tiny bubbles appear on the bottom and the walls. 4. Ask your child what is inside them.
flow.say: The water is only warm, and tiny bubbles have come. What do you think is inside them? Where did it come from?
flow.kid: Watch the pan from an arm's length away. Tiny bubbles come first. What do you think is inside them?
flow.parent: These first bubbles are air that was dissolved in the tap water. Warm water holds less dissolved air than cold water, so the air comes out.
flow.context: This is the first step of What Is in the Bubbles? Here you watch the tiny bubbles that appear when water is only warm.

flow.do: 1. Keep heating until big bubbles rise from the bottom and the water rolls. 2. Ask what is inside these bubbles. 3. The grown-up holds the cold plate with the cloth, about 30 cm above the pan, for 5 seconds. 4. Show your child the underside of the plate.
flow.say: Now the bubbles are big and they keep coming. Are these air too? Look under the plate. What is on it?
flow.kid: Now the water boils. Big bubbles rise from the bottom. What is in them? Look under the cold plate.

ask.q: If the big bubbles were air, what would run out after a while?
good: The air. But the bubbles keep coming as long as the pan is heated.

flow.context: This step of What Is in the Bubbles? is the boil. You watch the big bubbles and catch what leaves the pan on a cold plate.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the stove. 2. Watch how soon the big bubbles stop. 3. Ask your child to say what each kind of bubble was, and how they know.
flow.say: The moment the heat stopped, the big bubbles stopped. What does that tell you about them? What were the two kinds of bubbles?
flow.kid: The stove is off. Do the big bubbles go on? Say what each kind of bubble was.
flow.parent: The big bubbles are water vapour. Water turned into a gas at the hot bottom of the pan. They stop when the heat stops, and the plate shows that water left the pan.

check.q: What is inside the big bubbles that rise in boiling water?
options: Water vapour
Air from the room
Nothing at all
check.why: The big bubbles are water that has turned into a gas inside the liquid. The plate above the pan gets wet as that gas condenses. The tiny early bubbles are dissolved air, and they are gone long before the boil.

flow.context: This is the last step of What Is in the Bubbles? Here you say what was inside the small early bubbles and the big bubbles of boiling water.

activities.title: Zoom In on the Water Cycle
activities.context: In this activity you draw the water cycle, and then add six zoom circles. Each circle shows what the particles of water are doing at that place.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper, or two sheets taped together
pencils or crayons, with red and blue among them
a steel tumbler to draw circles round
your drawing from Draw the Particles, if you have done it

activities.record: Keep the finished picture on a wall. Tell the journey of one particle to someone who has not seen it.

setup.art: A large sheet with a sea on the left, the Sun above, a cloud over hills on the right and a river running back to the sea.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the sea, the Sun, a cloud, hills and a river.

setup.art: The same picture with six empty circles drawn at the sea surface, in the air, in the cloud, under the cloud, on the hill and in the river, numbered 1 to 6.
setup.caption: 2. Add six zoom circles along the journey.

setup.art: One zoom circle filled in: a water surface with two long-arrowed particles leaving and small squares of salt staying below.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the particles in each circle.

flow.do: 1. Draw the sea on the left and the Sun above it. 2. Draw hills on the right, with a cloud over them. 3. Draw a river from the hills back to the sea. 4. Add four big arrows: up from the sea, across to the hills, down as rain, and back along the river.
flow.say: First draw the whole journey. Where does the water go up? Where does it come down? How does it get back?
flow.kid: Draw the sea, the Sun, hills, a cloud and a river. Add four arrows to show where the water goes.
flow.parent: Label the arrows evaporation, wind, precipitation and river. Precipitation means rain, snow or hail.
flow.context: This is the first step of Zoom In on the Water Cycle. Here you draw the whole round journey of water, from the sea to a cloud and back.

flow.do: 1. Draw six circles with the tumbler, along the journey. Put one at the sea surface, one in the clear air and one where the cloud forms. Put one under the cloud, one on the hilltop and one in the river. 2. Number them 1 to 6. 3. Ask your child to draw the water particles in each. 4. Add a red arrow where energy goes into the water, and a blue one where it comes out.
flow.say: In each circle, draw what the water particles are doing. Are they close or far apart? Fast or slow? Where does energy go in, and where does it come out?
flow.kid: Draw six circles along the journey. Draw the water particles in each one. Are they close or far apart?
flow.parent: In circle 1, fast particles leave the sea, and the salt stays behind. In circle 2, vapour particles are far apart among the particles of air. In circle 3, slowed particles stick to a speck of dust. In circle 4, a raindrop holds many particles together. In circle 5, snow or hail on a cold hilltop has its particles in rows. In circle 6, liquid water is flowing. Draw a red arrow at circle 1 and a blue arrow at circle 3.
flow.context: This is the main step of Zoom In on the Water Cycle. Here you draw what the particles of water are doing at six places on their journey.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to put a finger on circle 1. 2. They tell the journey of one particle aloud, circle by circle. 3. Ask where the particle changes state. 4. Ask what happened to the salt of the sea.
flow.say: Be one particle of water. Start in the sea and tell me your whole journey. Where do you change state? What do you leave behind?
flow.kid: Put your finger on circle 1. You are one water particle. Tell your journey aloud, circle by circle.

ask.q: Where does the particle change state?
good: At the sea surface, from liquid to gas.
In the cloud, from gas to liquid.
On a cold hilltop, it may freeze into snow and later melt.

flow.think: A particle of water stays in the air for about 9 days. Where might a particle that left the Arabian Sea today come down?

check.q: In the water cycle, where do particles of water vapour slow down and join into drops?
options: High up, where the air is cold
At the surface of the warm sea
In the river, on the way back
check.why: Rising air cools. Cold slows the vapour particles until they stick to specks of dust and to each other, and a cloud forms. At the sea surface the opposite happens: fast particles leave the liquid.

flow.context: This is the last step of Zoom In on the Water Cycle. Here you tell the journey of one particle of water aloud, and say where it changes state.

activities.title: Find the Dew Point (if you have a thermometer)
activities.context: In this activity you cool a steel tumbler of water slowly with ice. You read a thermometer at the moment mist first forms on the outside. That temperature is the dew point of the air in your room.

materials.item: a shiny steel tumbler, dry on the outside
tap water
ice cubes
a room, kitchen or laboratory thermometer that reads from 0 to 50 degrees Celsius (a fever thermometer will not work)
a spoon and a dry cloth
a weather app that shows the dew point

activities.record: Write the room, the time, the temperature at which mist first formed, and the dew point from the weather app.

setup.art: A shiny steel tumbler half full of water with a thermometer standing in it, on a table beside a bowl of ice cubes.
setup.caption: 1. Half fill a dry steel tumbler and read the temperature.

setup.art: A hand dropping one ice cube into the tumbler while another hand stirs with a spoon.
setup.caption: 2. Add one ice cube at a time, and stir until it melts.

setup.art: A close view of the outside of the tumbler with the first faint band of mist at the level of the water, and the thermometer reading 22.
setup.caption: 3. Read the thermometer the moment mist first appears.

flow.do: 1. Half fill the tumbler with tap water and dry its outside well. 2. Stand the thermometer in it and read the temperature. 3. Ask your child at what temperature mist will form on the outside, and why they think so. 4. Write the guess.
flow.say: We will cool this water a little at a time. At what temperature do you think the outside will mist over? Why?
flow.kid: Half fill the tumbler. Dry the outside. Read the thermometer. Guess when mist will form. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Find the Dew Point. Here you read the starting temperature of a tumbler of water and guess when mist will form on it.

flow.do: 1. Add one ice cube and stir gently until it has melted. 2. Look at the outside of the tumbler, at the level of the water. Keep your face away, because breath makes mist too. 3. If the steel is still clear, add another cube and stir again. 4. At the first faint mist, read the thermometer and write the number.
flow.say: Stir, then look closely at the steel. Is it still shiny? Tell me the moment it turns dull.
flow.kid: Add one ice cube. Stir until it melts. Look at the outside. Is it misty yet? If not, add another cube.
flow.parent: Wipe a finger across the steel to check. A clear streak in a dull patch means mist. In a humid room it may form after one or two cubes. In very dry air there may be no mist even near 2 degrees. Then the dew point is lower than that.
flow.context: This is the main step of Find the Dew Point. Here you cool the water one ice cube at a time and read the temperature when mist first forms.

flow.do: 1. Compare your number with the dew point in the weather app. 2. If you can, do the test again in the bathroom just after a bath. 3. Ask your child why the two rooms gave different numbers.
flow.say: Your number is the dew point of this room. How close is it to the weather app's? Why would a steamy bathroom give a higher number?
flow.kid: Look at the dew point in the weather app. Is your number close to it? Why might a bathroom be different?
flow.parent: Your number is often 1 to 3 degrees below the app's. The steel is a little warmer than the water inside. Indoor air can also differ from outdoor air, above all with an air conditioner on.

check.q: Mist formed on one tumbler at 24 degrees and on another, in a different room, at 12 degrees. Which room had more water vapour in its air?
options: The room where mist formed at 24 degrees
The room where mist formed at 12 degrees
Both had the same amount
check.why: Air with a lot of vapour needs only a little cooling before the vapour condenses. So its dew point is high. Dry air must be cooled much further.

flow.context: This is the last step of Find the Dew Point. Here you compare your own measurement with the dew point given by a weather app.

projects.title: The Evaporation Survey: how do ten people use evaporation?
projects.context: In this three-day project you ask ten people how they use evaporation in daily life. You tally their answers, draw a bar chart and say what you found.

materials.item: paper, a pencil and a ruler
people to ask: family, neighbours, or relatives on the phone

schedule.what: Make a data sheet with eight ways of using evaporation. Guess which way most people use.
Ask ten people which of the eight ways they use, and tally the answers.
Draw a bar chart, write what you found, and say how the survey could be better.

projects.record: Keep the data sheet with its tally marks and the bar chart. Write three sentences: the most used way, the least used way, and one thing that surprised you.

setup.art: A hand-ruled sheet with eight rows, each naming a use of evaporation, and empty columns for tally marks.
setup.caption: 1. Make a data sheet with eight ways of using evaporation.

setup.art: A child with a clipboard asking a woman who is hanging washing on a terrace line, and making a tally mark.
setup.caption: 2. Ask ten people and make a tally mark for each yes.

setup.art: A bar chart with eight bars of different heights, drawn in pencil and coloured in.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a bar for each way.

flow.do: 1. Rule a sheet with eight rows. 2. Write one way of using evaporation in each row. Use the list in the note below, or your child's own ideas. 3. Add a column for tally marks and a column for totals. 4. Ask your child which way most people will say yes to, and why.
flow.say: People use evaporation every day, often without naming it. Which of these eight ways do you think the most people use? Why?
flow.kid: Rule eight rows. Write one way of using evaporation in each. Guess which one most people use. Say why.
flow.parent: Eight ways: drying clothes on a line. Drying hair. Drying food in the sun, such as vadam, papad, chillies or fish. Keeping water cool in a clay pot. Using an air cooler with wet pads. Sprinkling water on a floor, a yard or a roof to cool it. Drying a mopped floor under the fan. Boiling milk or sugarcane juice down to thicken it.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Evaporation Survey. Here you make a data sheet with eight ways people use evaporation, and guess which is most common.

flow.do: 1. Ask each of ten people the same question for every row: do you use evaporation in this way? 2. Make one tally mark for each yes. 3. Ask each person one more question: is there a way you used as a child and do not use now?
flow.say: Ask everyone in exactly the same words. Why does that matter in a survey?
flow.kid: Ask ten people about each row. Make a tally mark for each yes. Ask them all in the same words.
flow.context: This step of The Evaporation Survey collects the answers. You ask ten people which ways of using evaporation they use, and tally each yes.

flow.do: 1. Count the tally marks in each row. 2. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each way. 3. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why it came out that way. 4. Ask how the survey could be made better.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it came out that way. If you did this again, what would you change?
flow.kid: Count the tally marks. Draw a bar for each way. Say what you found. How could the survey be better?

ask.q: How could the survey be better?
good: Ask more people, because ten is a small number.
Ask people of different ages and from different places.
Ask about the season, because people dry things differently in the monsoon.

check.q: Ten people in one building were asked how they use evaporation. Nine dry clothes on a line. What is the fairest thing to say?
options: Most of the people asked dry clothes on a line
Everyone in India dries clothes on a line
Nobody uses a clothes dryer
check.why: A survey tells you about the people who were asked. Ten people in one building cannot speak for a whole country, and one of the ten gave a different answer.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Evaporation Survey. Here you draw a bar chart of the answers and say what the survey shows.

challenges.title: More Drops per Hour: build a better fresh-water maker (if you have a sunny balcony or window)
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. A bowl of salty water covered with clear film makes a little fresh water in the sun. It works by evaporation and condensation. Here you change the design so that it makes more.
challenges.problem: Build two fresh-water makers and stand them side by side in the sun for 3 hours. One is the plain design. The other is your improved design. Each starts with 1 tumbler of salty, coloured water. Make your improved one collect more fresh water than the plain one.
constraints: Both start with the same water: 1 tumbler of water with 1 teaspoon of salt and a spoonful of black tea for colour.
Both stand in the same sunshine for the same 3 hours.
Use only the Sun for heat. No stove and no hot water.
The collected water must be clear. If it is brown, salty water has splashed in.
materials: two large bowls of about the same size
clear cling film, or a clear plastic bag cut open
salt, black tea and tap water
things to try: a black cloth, a steel plate, a wet cloth, a wider tray
challenges.safety: Do not drink the collected water. The film and the bowls may not be clean enough.
general: Stand the bowl on a black cloth, or use a dark bowl. Dark things take in more sunlight, so the water gets warmer.
Use a wider bowl or tray, so that the salty water has a bigger surface.
Put a heavier stone on the film. The film then slopes more steeply, and the drops run to the middle sooner.
creative: Prop a shiny steel plate behind the bowl, to throw extra sunlight onto it.
Lay a ring of wet cloth round the edge of the film. A cooler film condenses vapour faster.
Hang a strip of black cloth with one end in the salty water. The wet cloth adds more surface for evaporation.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own improvement. Change one thing at a time if you can. How many teaspoons did each maker collect? Which change helped, and how do you explain it with particles?

setup.art: A large bowl with brown salty water in the bottom and an empty steel katori standing in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Pour the salty, coloured water round an empty katori in a big bowl.

setup.art: The bowl covered with clear film tied with string, and a small stone on the film making it dip above the katori.
setup.caption: 2. Cover with clear film. Put a stone on the film, above the katori.

setup.art: Two such bowls side by side on a sunny balcony, one standing on a black cloth with a steel plate propped behind it.
setup.caption: 3. Stand the plain maker and your improved one side by side in the sun.

setup.art: A child lifting a katori with a little clear water in it and measuring the water with a teaspoon.
setup.caption: 4. After 3 hours, measure the clear water in each katori.

flow.do: 1. Stir 1 teaspoon of salt and a spoonful of black tea into 1 tumbler of water. Make two tumblers like this. 2. Stand an empty katori in the middle of each big bowl. 3. Pour one tumbler of the brown water round each katori. 4. Cover each bowl with clear film and tie it. 5. Put a stone on each film, above the katori.
flow.say: This is the plain fresh-water maker. Where will the water evaporate? Where will it condense? How will the drops reach the katori?
flow.kid: Make two tumblers of brown, salty water. Stand a katori in each bowl. Pour the water round it. Cover with film. Add a stone.

good: Under the film, because the film is cooler than the warm, damp air inside.

flow.context: This is the first step of More Drops per Hour. Here you build two plain fresh-water makers from a bowl, a katori and clear film.

flow.do: 1. Read the usual ideas and the creative ideas together. 2. Ask your child to choose one or two changes for the second maker, and say why each should help. 3. Make the changes. 4. Stand both makers side by side in full sun. Note the time.
flow.say: What will you change to get more drops? Will your change speed up the evaporation, or the condensation? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Choose a change for one maker. Say why it should help. Make the change. Put both makers in the sun.
flow.parent: Ideas that warm the water or widen its surface speed up evaporation. Ideas that cool the film speed up condensation. Both give more drops.
flow.wait: Leave both makers in the sun for 3 hours
flow.context: This step of More Drops per Hour is the design step. You choose how to change one fresh-water maker so that it collects more water.

flow.do: 1. Look at both makers once every hour, without opening them. 2. Ask where the drops are forming. 3. Check that each stone is still above its katori.
flow.say: Look under the film. Where are the drops biggest? Which maker has more?
flow.kid: Look at both makers every hour. Do not open them. Where are the drops? Which has more?
flow.context: This step of More Drops per Hour is the hourly check. You look for drops under the film of each fresh-water maker.

flow.do: 1. After 3 hours, take off the films. 2. Lift out each katori and measure its water with the teaspoon. 3. Check that the water is clear. 4. Ask your child to explain the result with particles, and to say what they would change next.
flow.say: How many teaspoons did each one collect? Is the water clear? Where did the salt and the colour stay? What would you change next?
flow.kid: Lift out each katori. Measure the water with a teaspoon. Is it clear? Which maker collected more? Say why.
flow.parent: In strong sun the plain maker collects about 1 to 4 teaspoons in 3 hours. A good change can double that. On a hazy day both collect little, so try again on a clear day.

check.q: A fresh-water maker collected clear water from brown, salty water. Why was the collected water clear?
options: Only water particles evaporate
The film strains out the colour
Sunlight destroys salt and tea
check.why: Only particles of water leave the surface. The salt and the colour stay behind in the bowl. The vapour condenses under the film as pure water. Nothing passes through the film, and sunlight does not destroy the salt.

flow.context: This is the last step of More Drops per Hour. Here you measure the fresh water collected by the plain maker and by your improved one.

challenges.title: Catch Water from the Air
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about condensation. A steel tumbler of iced water gets wet on the outside, with water from the air. Here you design a way to collect as much of that water as you can.
challenges.problem: Use 12 ice cubes and things from the kitchen. Collect as much water from the air as you can in 20 minutes. Run your design beside a plain one, a single steel tumbler holding 12 ice cubes and water, and beat it.
constraints: Each design gets exactly 12 ice cubes.
Count only the water that forms on the outside of cold things. Ice and melted ice must stay inside.
Each design gets the same 20 minutes, in the same room.
Collect the water from each design with one dry handkerchief.
materials: steel tumblers, bowls, plates and lids
two dry trays or large plates to stand the designs on
two dry handkerchiefs of the same kind
the hanger balance from The Tilting Hanger, or a coat hanger and two clothes clips
general: Share the ice between three or four tumblers, so that more cold steel touches the air.
Add tap water to the ice. Then the whole wall of the tumbler is cold, and not just a few spots.
Run the test in the dampest room: the kitchen while rice is cooking, or the bathroom after a bath.
creative: Rest a large steel plate on a bowl of ice, tilted so that the drops run to one edge.
Stand the design under a fan. Moving air brings fresh vapour particles to the cold surface.
Stir a spoon of salt into the ice and water. Salty ice water is colder than plain ice water.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own water catcher. Which handkerchief ended up heavier, yours or the plain one's? What gave your design more cold surface, or more vapour?

setup.art: A single steel tumbler full of ice and water standing on a dry tray, its outside covered in drops.
setup.caption: 1. The plain design: one tumbler with 12 ice cubes and water.

setup.art: Four steel tumblers on a second tray, each with three ice cubes and water, and a tilted steel plate resting on a bowl of ice beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Your design: more cold surface for the vapour to land on.

setup.art: A child wiping the outside of a wet tumbler with a handkerchief, with a coat-hanger balance hanging behind.
setup.caption: 3. After 20 minutes, wipe each design with its own dry handkerchief.

setup.art: Two damp handkerchiefs clipped to the ends of a coat hanger, one end lower than the other.
setup.caption: 4. Hang the two handkerchiefs on the balance. Which is heavier?

flow.do: 1. Put 12 ice cubes in one steel tumbler, fill it with tap water and stand it on a dry tray. This is the plain design. 2. Read the problem and the ideas together. 3. Ask your child to plan a design for the other 12 ice cubes. Ask why it will catch more water.
flow.say: The drops on this tumbler came out of the air. How could 12 ice cubes catch more? What does the vapour need in order to condense?
flow.kid: Put 12 ice cubes and water in one tumbler. That is the plain design. Plan a better one. Say why it will catch more.

ask.q: What does the vapour need in order to condense?
good: A surface that is cold enough.
More cold surface means more places for particles to slow down and stick.

flow.context: This is the first step of Catch Water from the Air. Here you set up one plain tumbler of ice. You plan a design that will collect more water from the air.

flow.do: 1. Build the design on the second dry tray, in the same room. 2. Note the time. 3. Wait 20 minutes without touching either design. 4. Watch where the drops form first.
flow.say: Watch both designs. Where do the first drops form? Do they form above the level of the ice water, or only below it?
flow.kid: Build your design on the second tray. Wait 20 minutes. Do not touch. Watch where the drops form first.
flow.parent: Drops form only where the steel is cold, up to the level of the water inside. In a dry or air-conditioned room very little forms. A humid kitchen gives much more.
flow.context: This step of Catch Water from the Air runs the test. Your design and the plain tumbler stand side by side for 20 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Wipe all the outside water from the plain design, and from its tray, with one dry handkerchief. 2. Do the same for your design with the other handkerchief. 3. Clip one handkerchief to each end of the hanger balance. 4. See which end goes down. 5. Ask your child to explain the result and to suggest one more change.
flow.say: Which handkerchief is heavier? So which design caught more water from the air? What would you change next?
flow.kid: Wipe each design with its own dry handkerchief. Clip both to the hanger. Which end goes down? Say why.
flow.parent: In The Tilting Hanger, a coat hanger showed which of two wet cloths was heavier. Level it with both dry handkerchiefs before this test starts. A design with three or four tumblers usually wins clearly.

check.q: Twelve ice cubes shared between four steel tumblers collected more water from the air than twelve in one tumbler. Why?
options: More cold surface touched the air
Four tumblers hold more ice
Small tumblers make water
check.why: Vapour condenses only where it meets a cold surface. Four tumblers have about four times the cold steel of one. The amount of ice was the same, and no vessel makes water.

flow.context: This is the last step of Catch Water from the Air. Here you compare the water collected by two designs. You weigh two handkerchiefs on a hanger balance, as in The Tilting Hanger.

items.p: Where does evaporation happen in a tumbler of water?
items.why: Only particles at the surface can break away into the air. Choosing 'all through the water' mixes evaporation up with boiling.

items.p: True or false: water evaporates only when it is hot.
items.why: False. A wet floor dries in a cool room. At any temperature, a few particles at the surface are fast enough to escape.

items.p: When water vapour turns back into liquid water, the change is called ____.
a: condensation
items.why: Condensation is a gas turning into a liquid. It is the reverse of evaporation.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These five words carry the whole unit. A strong answer could give a home example of each.
pairs: a liquid turning into a gas at its surface
a gas turning into a liquid
how much water vapour is in the air

items.p: Does it speed up evaporation or slow it down?
items.why: Warmth, a bigger surface, moving air and dry air all let more particles leave than land back. Their opposites slow drying.

items.p: A plate and a tumbler hold the same water. Explain why the plate loses more in a day.
items.a: Water leaves only from its surface. The plate gives the water a much bigger surface, so many more particles are at the surface. More of them escape each second.
items.why: A strong answer says that the amount of water is the same. The size of the surface is what differs.

items.p: Which particles escape from the surface of water?
items.why: A particle needs enough speed to break away from its neighbours. All water particles are the same size, so 'the largest' cannot be right.

items.p: Draw the particles of liquid water and of water vapour in two boxes of the same size.
items.a: In the box of liquid water, draw many particles, touching and jumbled. In the box of water vapour, draw only one or two particles, far apart, with arrows to show them flying.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps the particles the same size in both boxes, and leaves the vapour box almost empty.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, labelled liquid water and water vapour.

items.p: Three of these are precipitation. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Rain, snow and hail fall from clouds. Dew does not fall. It condenses straight onto cool leaves and metal.

items.p: True or false: the water in a tightly capped bottle slowly gets less.
items.why: False. Particles still leave the water, but they cannot get away. As many land back as leave, so the level stays the same.

items.p: Put these steps of the water cycle in order, starting at the sea.
a: The Sun warms the sea
Water evaporates from the sea
The vapour rises and cools
The vapour condenses into cloud drops
Drops join and fall as rain
Rivers carry the water back to the sea
items.why: Energy from the Sun starts the journey. Evaporation takes the water up, condensation makes the cloud, and precipitation and rivers bring it back.
items: Drops join and fall as rain
Rivers carry the water back to the sea
The vapour condenses into cloud drops

items.p: Label a drawing of a pan of boiling water: bubbles of water vapour, invisible vapour, white cloud of tiny drops.
a: Bubbles of water vapour, rising inside the water
Invisible vapour, in the clear gap just above the water
White cloud of tiny liquid drops, higher up
items.why: The white cloud is not vapour. It is vapour that has condensed into tiny drops in the cooler air.
items.art: A pan of boiling water on a stove with bubbles inside, a clear gap above the surface and a white cloud higher up, with three blank label lines.

items.p: Two children watch hot milk cool in a wide davara. They explain it in different ways.
items.a: A strong answer says that both happen. In The Oil Lid, the bowl under oil still cooled. So heat does flow out through the steel and the oil. But the open bowl cooled faster, so evaporation carries away heat as well.
items.why: Neither child is wrong. The Oil Lid separates the two ways of cooling, because the oil stops only the evaporation.

views.says: The milk cools because its heat flows into the cooler air and the steel.
The milk cools because its fastest particles escape from the surface as vapour.

items.ask: Which child do you agree with, or are both right? Use The Oil Lid as evidence. Then say what the other child has noticed.

items.p: A fan dries a wet floor faster. What does the moving air do?
opts: Heats the water on the floor
items.why: Moving air sweeps away the vapour above the floor, so fewer particles land back. A fan does not heat the water.

items.p: Name two ways your family uses evaporation at home. For each, say what evaporates.
items.a: For example: we dry clothes on the balcony, and the water in the cloth evaporates. We keep drinking water in a clay pot, and water that seeps through the clay evaporates and cools the pot.
items.why: A strong answer names a real use and says which liquid leaves, and where it goes.

items.p: One water surface is 300 square cm and another is 75. How much more water does the bigger one lose?
items.why: 300 ÷ 75 = 4. Water leaves only from the surface, so 4 times the surface loses about 4 times the water.

items.p: In The Oil Lid, two bowls of water started equally hot. Explain why the open bowl ended cooler.
items.a: In the open bowl the fastest particles at the surface kept escaping as vapour. The particles left behind were slower on average, so the water was cooler. The oil stopped particles escaping from the other bowl.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of fast and slow particles, and says what the oil did.

items.p: True or false: at one temperature, all the particles of water move at the same speed.
items.why: False. They move at many different speeds. The temperature tells only how fast they move on average.

items.p: The temperature at which the vapour in the air starts to condense is called the ____ ____.
a: dew point
items.why: Humid air has a high dew point, and dry air has a low one.

items.p: For each change, does heat go into the water or come out of it?
items.why: Particles need energy to break away from each other, and they give it out when they join again. Dew forming is condensation.

items.p: When does sweat cool your body?
opts: When it stays on the skin
items.why: Sweat cools you only as it evaporates, because the fastest particles take heat away. Sweat that drips off carries almost no heat with it.

items.p: Draw the surface of the water inside a closed jar. Show particles leaving and particles landing back.
items.a: A water surface under a lid, with a few arrows going up from it. The same number of arrows come down onto it.
items.why: A strong drawing shows as many particles landing as leaving. That is why the level in a closed jar does not fall.
items.art: A jar with a lid, half full of water, with empty space above the water.

items.p: A lake in a dry state loses much water to evaporation. Three people disagree about covering it.
items.a: A strong answer uses the science: a cover stops particles leaving the surface, so it does save water. It also weighs what the cover changes for living beings, or where the vapour would have gone. Then it answers another view fairly.
items.why: All three views are held by real experts. Small tanks and canals are easier to cover than living lakes.

views.says: Cover it with floating panels. Every litre saved is a litre for a town or a field.
Leave it open. A cover blocks the light and air that fish, plants and birds need.
Evaporation cools the land and feeds the rain. Fix leaking pipes first.

items.ask: Choose the view you agree with most. Give one reason from the science of evaporation. Then answer one of the other two views.

items.p: These are the steps of a fair test of surface area. Put them in order.
a: Measure the same amount of water into each vessel
Stand all the vessels in the same place
Wait one day
Pour each one back and measure it
Compare the water lost with the size of the surface
items.why: The same water and the same place keep the test fair. Only then can the loss be put down to the surface.
items: Compare the water lost with the size of the surface
Stand all the vessels in the same place
Measure the same amount of water into each vessel
Pour each one back and measure it

items.p: Match each thing you see to what the particles are doing.
items.why: Every one of these has the same cause underneath: how many particles leave the liquid and how many come back.
pairs: more particles are at the surface
vapour particles slow down and stick

items.p: Tiny bubbles appear in a pan while the water is only warm. What are they?
items.why: Tap water holds dissolved air, and warm water holds less of it. Bubbles of water vapour come much later, at the boil.

items.p: A friend says, 'The Sun pulls the water out of wet clothes.' Explain what really happens, using particles.
items.a: The Sun does not pull. Sunlight warms the water in the cloth, so its particles move faster. More of them are fast enough to escape from the surface into the air as vapour.
items.why: A strong answer replaces 'pulls' with what the particles do, and says where the water goes.

items.p: Three of these make a wet cloth dry faster. Which one makes it dry more slowly?
items.why: Humid air already holds a lot of vapour, so many particles land back on the cloth. The other three speed up drying.

items.p: Label a drawing of the water cycle with these four words: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, river.
a: Evaporation: arrows rising from the sea
Condensation: where the cloud forms
Precipitation: rain falling from the cloud
River: water flowing back to the sea
items.why: Evaporation and condensation are changes of state. Precipitation and the river only move the water.
items.art: A sea, a cloud over hills, rain and a river in a loop, with four blank label lines.

items.p: True or false: on one day, a deep lake and a shallow puddle lose about the same depth.
items.why: True. Each square centimetre of surface loses about the same amount. The puddle vanishes first only because it has little depth to lose.

items.p: A thermometer in a tumbler of water reads 30 degrees. Two scientists disagree about what that number is.
items.a: A strong answer uses the unit: evaporation lowers the temperature by removing the fastest particles, so temperature does come from the particles. It also sees that the average does real things that no single particle does.
items.why: Physicists and philosophers still argue about this. Both views fit every experiment.

views.says: Only the particles are real. Temperature is just our name for their average speed.
Temperature is as real as any particle. It melts ice and burns fingers.

items.ask: Which scientist do you agree with? Give a reason from this unit. Then say what the other scientist has right.

items.p: Twelve particles have an average speed of 3.5. The two fastest leave. What happens to the average of the rest?
items.why: Taking away the highest numbers always lowers the average of what is left. This is why evaporation cools water.

items.p: In Wide or Narrow, the tumbler lost less water than the size of its surface suggested. Give a reason.
items.a: The walls of the tumbler stand above the water. They shelter the surface from the fan, so damp air collects there. More particles land back on the water, and the tumbler loses less.
items.why: A strong answer finds something that differed besides the area: the high walls and the still, damp air inside them.

items.p: Rain, snow and hail are all kinds of ____.
a: precipitation
items.why: Precipitation is any water that falls from clouds to the ground, as a liquid or as ice.

items.p: True or false: once water is boiling, more heat makes it hotter.
items.why: False. Boiling water in an open pan stays at its boiling point. Extra heat turns more water into vapour.

items.p: Draw a cloud drop forming. Show a speck of dust and the water particles around it.
items.a: A speck of dust in the middle, with several water particles stuck to it and to each other. A few fast vapour particles are still flying nearby.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the particles sticking to the speck. Vapour needs something to condense on.
items.art: An empty circle labelled 'inside a cloud, very close up'.

items.p: Is it true of evaporation, of boiling, or of both?
items.why: Both turn a liquid into a gas and both take heat in. They differ in where they happen and at what temperature.
items: needs 100 degrees for water at sea level
a liquid turns into a gas

items.p: Air rising up a mountainside cools, and a cloud forms. Why does cooling make a cloud?
opts: Vapour particles slow down and join
The wind brings water from rivers
items.why: Cooling slows the vapour particles until they stick to dust specks and to each other. No new water is made. It was already in the air as vapour.

items.p: Mist formed on four tumblers at these temperatures. Put the rooms in order, from the dampest air to the driest.
a: Room A: mist at 26 degrees
Room B: mist at 19 degrees
Room C: mist at 12 degrees
Room D: mist at 4 degrees
items.why: The temperature at which mist forms is the dew point. The higher the dew point, the more vapour the air holds.

items.p: Plan a fair test: does salty water evaporate more slowly than plain water? Say what you change, keep and measure.
items.a: Change only the water: one vessel has plain water and one has salty water. Keep the same amount of water, the same kind of vessel, the same place and the same time. Measure how much water each has lost after a day.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, keeps at least three things the same, and names what is measured.

items.p: Match each living being to the way they use evaporation to cool down.
items.why: All of them lose water to the air, and the water takes heat with it.
pairs: fan thin films of water in the hive
opens tiny holes in the leaves

items.p: The sea loses about 3 mm of depth to evaporation every day. About how much is that in one year?
items.why: 3 mm × 365 days = 1,095 mm, which is a little more than 1 metre. Rain and rivers put the same amount back.

items.p: Some scientists report that light can free water particles without heat. What evidence would make you believe it?
items.a: For example: other laboratories repeat the test and get the same result. The scientists measure the heat very carefully, to show that heating cannot explain the extra evaporation. The effect changes with the colour of the light, as they predict.
items.why: A strong answer asks for the result to be repeated by others. It also asks for the ordinary explanation to be ruled out.

items.p: Three of these changes take heat in. Which one gives heat out?
items.why: When steam condenses, its particles join again and give out the energy they took in. That is why steam burns so badly.

items.p: Label a cut-through drawing of a wet clay pot wall: surface where water leaves, dry outer layer, wet middle.
a: Surface where water leaves: the outside face, touching the air
Dry outer layer: pale, just under the surface
Wet middle: dark, deep inside the wall
items.why: Water leaves only from the surface. The middle stays wet until its water has crept out to the surface.
items.art: A thick slice of clay wall drawn side-on, pale at the outer edge and dark in the middle, with three blank label lines.

quiz.p: A tumbler of water stands on a shelf, away from any heat. Why does its level slowly fall?
opts: Fast particles at the surface escape
The water shrinks as it gets old
The water leaks through the bottom
quiz.why: At any temperature a few particles at the surface are fast enough to leave. Steel does not soak up water, and water does not shrink with age.

quiz.p: Water at 30 degrees evaporates slowly, not all at once. What does this show about its particles?
opts: They move at many different speeds
They all move at one speed
They do not move at all
They are of many different sizes
quiz.why: Only a few are fast enough to escape at any moment. If all had one speed, all would leave together or none would.

quiz.p: Drops form on the outside of a cold steel tumbler. What happened to the particles of water vapour?
opts: They slowed down and stuck together
quiz.why: The cold steel took energy from the vapour particles. Slow particles stick together as a liquid. Nothing passes through steel.

quiz.p: A wet cloth dries faster on a dry day than on a humid day. Why?
opts: Fewer particles land back on it
quiz.why: Humid air holds a lot of vapour, so many particles land back on the cloth. Dry air has few to give back.

quiz.p: Which change would make a wet towel dry more slowly?
quiz.why: Folding hides most of the surface, and water can leave only from a surface that touches the air.

quiz.p: A bowl loses 6 mm of water a day. How much does a plate with 3 times the surface lose?
quiz.why: Three times the surface loses about three times the water. 6 × 3 = 18 mm. Choosing 6 mm treats the amount of water as what matters.

quiz.p: Why does evaporation cool the water that is left behind?
quiz.why: With the fastest gone, the average speed of the rest is lower, and that means a lower temperature. Cold is not a thing that enters.

quiz.p: A layer of oil stops hot water evaporating. How does that water cool, compared with an open bowl?
quiz.why: It still loses heat through the bowl, but it cannot lose its fastest particles. So it cools more slowly.

quiz.p: Which is true of boiling but not of evaporation?
opts: Bubbles of vapour form inside the liquid
A liquid turns into a gas
quiz.why: Evaporation happens only at the surface. In boiling, vapour forms all through the liquid. The other three are true of both.

quiz.p: In the water cycle, what happens to the salt when sea water evaporates?
quiz.why: Only particles of water leave the surface. That is why rain is fresh, though most of it rose from the salty sea.

quiz.p: Which list holds only kinds of precipitation?
quiz.why: Precipitation is water that falls from clouds. Dew and fog do not fall, and rivers and lakes are water already on the ground.

quiz.p: You test whether a fan speeds up drying. What must stay the same for both cloths?
opts: The cloth, the water and the warmth
Only the colour of the cloth
Nothing needs to stay the same
The fan must blow on both
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes: here, the moving air. If the fan blew on both, nothing would have been tested.

applications: Farmers dry paddy, pepper, coffee beans and red chillies in the sun. They spread them in a thin layer and turn them. A heap would stay wet inside and grow mould.
Salt makers in Thoothukudi and in Kutch let sea water into wide, shallow pans. The big surface lets the Sun and the wind take the water and leave the salt.
An air cooler blows room air through wet pads. Water evaporating from the pads cools the air. Coolers work well in dry Nagpur and poorly in humid Chennai.
Builders keep new concrete covered with wet gunny sacks for a week or more. Concrete needs its water to harden, so they slow the evaporation.
Sports clothes are woven to spread sweat into a thin film over a large surface. The sweat evaporates fast and cools the runner.
Attar makers in Kannauj heat rose petals in water in a copper pot. The vapour carries the scent along a bamboo pipe and condenses in a cooled vessel.
Power stations cool their hot water in tall cooling towers. The white plume above a tower is water vapour that has condensed into tiny drops.

open_questions.q: Can light free water particles from a surface without heating the water?
open_questions.why_open: A group in the United States reported this in 2023. Other laboratories have not yet repeated it fully, and some scientists suggest other explanations.

open_questions.q: Why has evaporation from weather-station pans fallen in many places, while the world has warmed?
open_questions.why_open: Records from many countries, including India, show less water lost from open pans than fifty years ago. Weaker winds and hazier skies explain a part of it. Scientists still argue about the rest.

open_questions.q: How do the first few particles of water join into a drop when there is nothing to stick to?
open_questions.why_open: The first cluster has only a handful of particles and lasts a tiny part of a second. It is too small and too quick to watch, and hard to calculate.

open_questions.q: Can drinking water be taken cheaply from dry desert air?
open_questions.why_open: New sponge-like materials can catch vapour at night and give it up as water in sunlight. They work in the laboratory. Nobody yet knows if they can be made cheaply enough for a village.

open_questions.q: Can evaporation be used to make electricity?
open_questions.why_open: Small engines driven by evaporating water have been built in laboratories since 2015. Lakes and reservoirs lose a huge amount of energy this way. Nobody knows yet whether it can be collected in a useful amount.

maths.problem: In Wide or Narrow, a bowl had a water surface of 75 square cm. It lost 7 mm of water in a day. A tray with a surface of 450 square cm stood beside it. About how much water did the tray lose?
maths.explain: The tray's surface is 450 ÷ 75 = 6 times as big as the bowl's. Water leaves only from the surface, so the tray loses about 6 times as much. 7 × 6 = 42 mm.
maths.context: This is about Wide or Narrow. In it, a wide plate had 4 times the surface of a bowl. The plate lost about 4 times as much water.
maths.why_maths: The loss grows in step with the surface. Once you know that, you can predict the loss from any vessel without waiting a day.

maths.problem: The water in a plate is 16 cm across. Use the three-quarters rule to find the area of its surface.
maths.explain: Multiply the width by itself: 16 × 16 = 256. A circle fills about three-quarters of the square round it. Three-quarters of 256 is 192. So the area is about 192 square cm.
maths.context: This is about Wide or Narrow, where you found the area of each round water surface from its width.
maths.why_maths: A ruler measures width, but evaporation depends on area. The rule turns the number you can measure into the number that matters.

maths.problem: In Wide or Narrow, a plate of 300 square cm lost 28 mm of water. A tumbler of 37 square cm lost 2 mm. If the tumbler had lost water as fast as the plate for its size, how much would it have lost? Why might it have lost less?
maths.answer: About 3.5 mm. The tumbler's tall walls shelter its water.
maths.explain: The plate's surface is about 300 ÷ 37 = 8 times the tumbler's. So the tumbler should lose about 28 ÷ 8 = 3.5 mm. It lost only 2 mm. Its walls stand above the water and keep the fan's air out. So damp air collects there, and more particles land back.
maths.context: This is about Wide or Narrow. In it, the same amount of water stood for a day in four vessels. They were a plate, a bowl, a tumbler and a closed jar.

chart.title: Made-up example: water lost in one day

maths.why_maths: The sum shows what to expect. A result that does not match the sum points to something else that differed, and that is worth explaining.

maths.problem: In a game of Fast Ones Leave, the top row holds the speeds 6, 2, 5 and 3. The middle row holds 4, 1, 6 and 3. The bottom row holds 2, 4, 5 and 1. What is the average speed at the start? What is it after round 1, when the 6 and the 5 in the top row have escaped?
maths.answer: 3.5 at the start, and 3.1 after round 1.
maths.explain: At the start the total is 16 + 14 + 12 = 42, and 42 ÷ 12 = 3.5. In round 1 the 6 and the 5 in the top row leave. The total is now 42 − 11 = 31, and 10 particles are left. 31 ÷ 10 = 3.1. The average has fallen, so the pot is cooler.
maths.context: This is about Fast Ones Leave, a dice game with a pot of twelve particles. In it, the fastest particles in the surface row escape.
maths.why_maths: No single particle shows the cooling. Only the average does, and an average has to be worked out.

maths.problem: In The Oil Lid, readings were taken every 5 minutes, from 0 to 20 minutes. The open bowl was cooler than the oil bowl by 0, 3, 5, 6 and 7 degrees. In which 5 minutes did the gap grow most? Predict the gap at 25 minutes, and give a reason.
maths.answer: The gap grew most in the first 5 minutes. At 25 minutes it would be about 7 or 8 degrees.
maths.explain: The gap grew by 3, then 2, then 1, then 1 degree. So it grows more slowly as time passes. One more step of about 1 degree, or less, gives 7 to 8 degrees. The reason is that the open bowl is cooler by then. Cooler water has fewer fast particles, so it evaporates more slowly.
maths.context: This is about The Oil Lid. In it, an open bowl of hot water cooled faster than a bowl whose water was sealed under oil.

chart.title: Made-up example: how much cooler the open bowl was

maths.why_maths: A line graph shows not only that the gap grows, but how its growth slows. That slowing is a clue to what the particles are doing.

maths.problem: Wide or Narrow was set up at 8:40 on Monday morning. The water was measured at 7:25 on Tuesday morning. For how long did the water stand? Was that more or less than one full day?
maths.answer: 22 hours and 45 minutes, which is 1 hour and 15 minutes less than a full day.
maths.explain: From 8:40 on Monday morning to 8:40 on Tuesday morning is 24 hours. 7:25 is 1 hour and 15 minutes before 8:40. 24 hours − 1 hour 15 minutes = 22 hours 45 minutes.
maths.context: This is about Wide or Narrow. In it, four vessels of water stood for about one day before the water was measured.
maths.why_maths: A loss of water means little unless you know how long it took. Two tests can be compared fairly only if their times are known.

maths.problem: In Fast Ones Leave, a particle in the surface row escapes if its speed is 5 or 6. What is the chance that one surface particle escapes? Of the 4 particles in a surface row, about how many escape in a round?
maths.answer: The chance is 2 in 6, which is 1 in 3. About 1 or 2 of the 4 escape.
maths.explain: A die has 6 faces, and 2 of them are a 5 or a 6. So the chance is 2 in 6, or 1 in 3. One-third of 4 is a little more than 1. So in most rounds 1 or 2 particles escape, and sometimes none.
maths.context: This is about Fast Ones Leave, a dice game. In it, a die gives each of twelve particles a speed from 1 to 6.
maths.why_maths: Nobody can say which particle will leave. Chance still tells you about how many will, and that is how real evaporation can be so steady.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that evaporating water mixes into the air as a gas of its own? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1700s most scientists explained evaporation like this: air dissolves water, just as water dissolves sugar. If that were right, water could not evaporate where there is no air. John Dalton was a teacher in Manchester, England, who wrote down the weather every day for 57 years. In 1801 he tested the idea. He let water evaporate into a glass tube that held almost no air. He did the same in a tube full of dry air, at the same temperature. Then he measured how hard the water vapour pushed in each tube. The push was the same. So the air was not dissolving the water. Dalton concluded that water vapour is a gas of its own. Its particles move about among the particles of the air without joining them. The air only gets in their way and slows them down. Thinking about these mixed gases led Dalton, a few years later, to his theory that all matter is made of atoms.
how_we_found_out.who: John Dalton, a teacher and weather recorder in Manchester, England
how_we_found_out.when: The experiments were done in 1801 and printed in 1802. His first printed table of atoms followed in 1805.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That water evaporates because air dissolves it, as water dissolves sugar. Dalton showed that water gives off the same amount of vapour into an almost empty tube as into air. So air is not needed for evaporation.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in plain dark clothes of about 1800 reading the height of mercury in two tall glass tubes on a wooden stand, with a weather diary open on the table.

roots.context: We have learned that the fastest particles of water escape at its surface. We have also learned that slow particles of vapour join into drops. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In The Oil Lid, the open bowl of hot water cooled faster than the bowl sealed with oil. Water particles move at many different speeds, and only the fastest ones at the surface escape. The particles left behind are slower on average, so the water is cooler. So one temperature stands for many different speeds, and evaporation lowers it by removing the fastest.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'the water is at 30 degrees' as if every bit of the water were the same. A thermometer gives one number, so we picture every particle moving in the same way. The number is an average of particles that differ widely. What happens to the water depends on the few that are far from the average.
deep_truth.evidence: In The Oil Lid, two bowls began equally hot, and the bowl that could evaporate ended several degrees cooler. In Fast Ones Leave, the average speed of the pot fell whenever the 5s and 6s at the surface left. In Wide or Narrow, water kept leaving at room temperature, so some particles were always fast enough to escape.

three.who_am_i: Your body cools itself in this way. When sweat evaporates, its fastest particles leave your skin and take heat with them. You have one body temperature, held steady by losing fast particles all day.
three.what_is_life: A neem tree, a panting dog and a hive of bees all lose water to the air to stay cool. Each of them controls how much: the tree by opening leaf holes, the dog by panting, the bees by fanning.
three.what_is_this_world: The sea loses its fastest particles every second, more than a metre of depth each year. Those particles become every cloud, every river and all the rain. The fresh water on land is water that left the sea as vapour and came back as rain.

roots.thread: A tumbler of water looks like one still thing with one temperature. It is a vast crowd of particles, each moving at a speed of its own. The one temperature comes from all of them together. The few fastest leave, and from them come vapour, clouds and rain. Rain feeds the rivers, the trees and you. So the water cycle begins with the differences in speed between the particles inside the water.

teachings.source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things, Book 1 (Rome, about 55 BCE)
teachings.teaching: Clothes hung by the sea grow damp, and spread in the sun they dry. Nobody sees the water settle on them or leave them. So, Lucretius says, the water must come and go in pieces too small for the eye to see.
teachings.link: This is evaporation explained with particles, two thousand years before anyone could test it. Lucretius reasoned from washing on a line, as this unit does.

teachings.teaching: Unless drops fall from the sky, not even a blade of green grass will lift its head.
teachings.link: Every one of those drops was made by condensation, from particles that evaporated somewhere else. The verse tells us how much all living things depend on rain. The science tells us where the drops come from.

teachings.source: Milindapanha (The Questions of King Milinda), the chariot passage
teachings.teaching: The monk Nagasena asks the king whether the chariot is its wheels, its axle or its pole. It is none of them. 'Chariot' is a name for all the parts working together.
teachings.link: Temperature is like this. No single particle has it. It is a name for what a great many particles are doing together. The science does not prove the Buddhist teaching about the self, which Nagasena goes on to draw.

science.text: The particles of a gas or a liquid at one temperature move at a wide spread of speeds. James Clerk Maxwell worked out the spread in 1860.
Evaporation removes the most energetic particles, so it cools what is left. Physicists use the same method to cool gases to within a millionth of a degree of the coldest possible temperature.
Light may be able to knock water particles out of a surface without heating it first.

other_view.who: Many physicists and philosophers of science
other_view.view: An average is not less real than the particles. Temperature burns a finger, melts ice and drives the weather, and it can be measured without knowing anything about particles. A crowd has real features that none of its members has. So the temperature of the water is as real a thing as any particle in it.

practice.title: Sit with a warm tumbler
practice.say: Let's hold a tumbler of warm water in both hands and sit still. Feel the warmth in your palms. Now look at the surface of the water. You cannot see anything leaving. But the fastest particles are leaving every moment. Take ten slow breaths. Feel the tumbler grow a little less warm. Where has that warmth gone?
practice.kid: Hold a tumbler of warm water in both hands. Sit still. Feel the warmth. Look at the top of the water. The fastest particles are leaving right now. Take ten slow breaths. Is the tumbler less warm? Where did the warmth go?

ask: If you could follow every particle in a tumbler of water, would you still need the word 'temperature'?
The fastest particles leave the sea and become rain for the land. Is the rain still part of the sea?
Your body is warm because of how your particles move on average, and some of them are much faster and some much slower. So what is you: one particular particle, or all of them together?

playtest: Reasoned through step by step, as a parent and child in a city flat would do it. Not yet tried at home. Wide or Narrow (core) needs a clear straight-sided glass, a ruler, a rimmed steel plate, a bowl, a tumbler and a jar with a lid. It takes two days, with 24 minutes on the first and 21 on the second. Under a fan in dry weather the plate should lose 20 to 40 mm of height in the measuring glass. On a humid day it loses about 10 mm, and a second day of waiting helps. The plate should lose about 4 times as much as a bowl half as wide. The tumbler often loses less than its area suggests, because its walls shelter the water. The closed jar shows how much water is lost in pouring. The Oil Lid (core) needs a grown-up for the hot water, which is about 50 degrees. The oil must cover the whole surface, so a third spoonful may be needed. The open bowl should feel clearly cooler after 10 to 20 minutes, by about 4 to 8 degrees. It works on humid days too, because hot water evaporates fast into any room air. The Tilting Hanger depends on the weather. The lighter cloth's end should rise 1 to 4 cm after 8 minutes, and less on a very humid day. Tumbler or Davara and What Is in the Bubbles? need a grown-up. Shake the Plate loses 0 to 3 chana with a gentle shake and 8 to 20 with a hard one. Find the Dew Point needs a thermometer that reads from 0 to 50 degrees, and in very dry air no mist may form. More Drops per Hour needs 3 hours of strong sun, and collects only 1 to 4 teaspoons. Catch Water from the Air collects little in a dry or air-conditioned room, so a humid kitchen is better. Fast Ones Leave needs division to one decimal place, and a phone calculator is fine. No part needs a garden.
